articles.title: Sara Duterte's defense to Cabotaje-Tang: Are you anti-Duterte? A kakampink?
articles.summary: Defense counsel Atty. Mark Vinluan during his cross-examination also asked the former magistrate of the anti-graft court if she was anti-Duterte or was allied with the camp of former Vice President…

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 4:00pm

The defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte raised before the impeachment court the non-appointment of former Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang to the Supreme Court for which she applied during the administration of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Defense counsel Atty. Mark Vinluan during his cross-examination also asked the former magistrate of the anti-graft court if she was anti-Duterte or was allied with the camp of former Vice President Leni Robredo.

The prosecution had presented Cabotaje-Tang as an expert witness on public accountability. She testified that a public official’s acquisition of unexplained wealth can be a ground for removal from office.
“Are you anti-Duterte now?” Vinluan asked.
“No, I’m not,” Cabotaje-Tang replied.
“Do you like VP Sara?” Vinluan asked.
“I do not know her personally,” the former justice said.
Vinluan asked Cabotaje-Tang if she was a “kakampink,” or a member of the group which supported former Vice President Leni Robredo in the 2022 presidential elections.
Cabotaje-Tang said she was unfamiliar with the term.
After getting an explanation, she said, “No. I’ve never been political in my life. I’ve always been apolitical.”
Vinluan then asked if Cabotaje-Tang was friends with prosecutor Akbayan party-list Rep. Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno.
The subpoena for her attendance had been coursed through Diokno’s office.
“No. We were adversaries, actually, in the amparo cases before the Court of Appeals,” came the reply.

articles.title: Thames Water redraws mega-reservoir plan amid local opposition
articles.summary:
A new public consultation has opened on the 150bn-litre above-ground White Horse project in Abingdon, Oxfordshire

Thames Water has amended the blueprint of a

blocks.text: Thames Water has amended the blueprint of a planned mega-reservoir in Oxfordshire as the struggling utility tries to convince regulators that construction should go ahead amid warnings of “catastrophic consequences”.
The White Horse reservoir near Abingdon is scheduled to hold 150bn litresof water with a surface area of 6.7 sq km (2.6 sq miles) – almost the same size as Gatwick airport.

The estimated cost has rocketed from £2.2bn to between £5.5bn and £7.5bn after a review last year more than tripled the site to 38 sq km to accommodate extra building works, relocate adjacent solar farms and reroute local rivers and streams.

Thames Water said the scheme, formerly known as the South East Strategic Reservoir Option, needed “additional access points to carry out construction and environmental mitigation works, such as new habitat creation”, forcing it to carry out “targeted consultation with landowners, and those with an interest in land that may be impacted by this change”.

A public consultation into the original plans concluded in January. Last week, a further consultation began and is expected to end next month. Thames aims to submit a planning application by late 2026.
If approved, main works construction would begin in 2032 with water available by 2040, serving 15 million people.

Thames said the reservoir is needed to cope with the growing population in the south-east and the changing climate, which has put pressure on water resources in many parts of the UK, including during this summer’s heatwaves.

Rapid, a partnership between the industry regulator Ofwat, the Environment Agency and the Drinking Water Inspectorate, which oversees the early development of large-scale water infrastructure projects, said there was a projected shortfall of more than 2bn litres a day by 2055.
Campaigners have accused Thames Water of underestimating the reservoir’s cost and overstating its strategic value since plans for a 10 sq km, £1bn project were first put forward in 2006.

The reservoir has proved controversial after designs showed the facility would be largely above ground level and would need walls up to 25 metres high to contain the main body of water, making it the largest “fully bounded” reservoir in Europe.

blocks.caption: A campaign group says the reservoir is a flawed concept. Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Observer

blocks.text: The site is one of the few in the south of England with enough clay across a large area to build a reservoir, but the clay is only a few metres deep, forcing Thames to build the UK’s first walled reservoir structure.

The most recent estimates of costs are in 2023 prices, leading critics to say that after three years of high inflation, especially in the construction industry, the estimated cost of the White Horse reservoir is more likely to be £7.5bn-£10bn.
Customers of Thames Water, Affinity Water and Southern Water are due to pay for the new reservoir through their bills over the next 100 years.
after newsletter promotion

At the end of March, the regulated value of Thames’s assets was estimated at £23bn while its net debt increased to £18.5bn. Ministers are considering whether to put the company into special administration or accept a solution put forward by creditors to maintain private-sector control after a debt write-off.

The Vale of White Horse district council, Abingdon town council and Oxfordshire county council have rejected the plans, citing flood risks to neighbouring villages from rivers and streams on the site that will need to be diverted.

Derek Stork, chair of the Group Against Reservoir Development, said the reservoir was a flawed concept and there were more sustainable ways to supply water to the area. He said Thames Water had failed to consult adequately with local organisations, councils and residents.

“No dam breach analysis or comprehensive flood risk modelling has been shared, despite the reservoir’s location on a red-rated flood plain and the potential for catastrophic consequences in the event of failure,” he said. A red-rated area is at severe risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency.
A Thames Water spokesperson said: “This consultation is just the latest part of our ongoing programme of engagement around the project, which we have been undertaking for more than four years.
“The feedback we get, along with feedback gathered during our statutory public consultation last year, will help inform our proposals.”

articles.title: Carney is seeking trillions in investment at this week's summit. What will it take to land major deals?

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney visits the Davie shipyard in Lévis, Que., on Aug. 24. Carney's investment summit this week in Toronto will bring together deep-pocketed investors from around the globe, but experts say the government must work to show the country is serious about building big projects. (Sy

blocks.text: Business·New

Hundreds of high-profile international investors are meeting with business leaders in Toronto this week, in the hope of drumming up new investments. More than 167 major projects are on the table, but what will it take for Canadian leaders to show that the country is committed to building big things?
Long turnaround times and approval issues have previously turned some investors away from Canada
Hundreds of deep-pocketed investors have descended on Toronto for the first-of-its-kind Canada Investment Summit.
The summit, which began with a reception on Sunday, aims to bring together global investors with Canadian business leaders in the hopes of landing $1 trillion worth of investments across the country.

As a former central banker and head of Brookfield Asset Management, Prime Minister Mark Carney is no stranger to big-name investors. But the stakes are high, as the escalating Canada-U.S. trade war has turned up the pressure to forge new relationships, and prove that Canada is a good place to invest.
So, who is coming to the summit and what does Canada need to do to land new cash for its big projects? Here's what you need to know.
Who's coming?

CBC News previously reported that Carney invited 100 of the world's biggest investors to the summit. The government has kept the final guest list close to its chest, but some big names are reportedly on it.

Larry Fink, chairman of BlackRock Inc. — a U.S.-based investment firm and the world's largest asset manager — and Dilhan Pillay, CEO of the Singapore-based investment firm Temasek, are some of them. Managers of massive sovereign wealth funds including Norway's government pension fund and state-owned firms like the Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. will also be there.

"It's essentially a who's-who on the investment side," said Jeremy Kronick, president and CEO of the C.D. Howe Institute, the economic think-tank, with plenty more banks and money managers from Canada and abroad expected to attend.
Carney invites major investors to discuss opportunities in Canada
What projects are on the table?

Some 167 projects, ranging from a proposed pipeline carrying oil from Alberta to B.C.'s coast to developing satellite technology for Earth observation, are among the investment opportunities on the table, according to a 66-page prospectus obtained by CBC News.

The prospectus groups projects into eight types: 11 conventional energy projects, 31 clean energy ones, 63 in mining and metals, 16 in marine and port infrastructure, 11 others in power and utilities, 10 in digital technology, 19 in advanced manufacturing and six transportation projects.
More than half of them are related to energy and mining, which Kronick says shows where the government's priorities lie.

Some of the most expensive and highest-profile projects on the list include that $35-billion pipeline to B.C., a roughly $79-billion expansion of the Port of Churchill in northern Manitoba and the proposed $28.5-billion Ksi Lisims liquid natural gas terminal on the B.C. coast.
Why do we need it?
The goal is to show Canada off as a "compelling investment destination," as the government puts it — even though that hasn't always been the case.
Kronick says long turnaround times for big projects and uncertainty about whether they will get approved have turned some international investors off of Canadian projects in the past.

A recent report by the CPP Investment Insights Institute — the research arm of the firm which is helping lead the summit — collected responses from 65 global institutional investors about their perceptions around a number of developed countries.

Canada ranked highest in stability and regulatory predictability, and the investors said they saw opportunity in Canada's critical minerals, energy and other resources. But regulatory complexity and permitting timelines were big concerns, especially among those interested in mining and energy projects, according to the report.

Because Canada is considered a small economy, Kronick says more work needs to be done to make it a competitive option compared to other developed nations. And hosting a summit like this — to signal the country is serious about building big things — is a good start.
"I think the change in tone is welcome," Kronick said. "It's been missing in the last number of years."
He says business leaders here must show that Canada is serious about the major projects on the table, with the man-power and machinery ready to get them built quickly.
Even if deals don't materialize quickly, Kronick says any that come down the line could boost Canada's productivity and GDP in a big way.

If the government plays its cards right, a report from TD Bank predicts Canada could see an investment "supercycle" that lasts a decade or longer, creating jobs and boosting real output per capita by $12,000 per person.
Why foreign investment?
But for some, the idea of foreign investment raises worries that companies abroad will have too much control over Canadian projects.
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis, for one, has criticized Carney's investment summit as a plan to "save this country by selling it off."
A protest counter-summit is also planned to coincide with the event. Organizers argue the government will "auction off" public resources in any deals it makes with outside firms.
'We have to use what leverage we have': NDP leader on U.S. trade war escalation
And indeed, not all foreign money is created equal, says Walid Hejazi, an economics professor at the Rotman School of Management in Toronto, who focuses on foreign investment.

He says there are always perceived risks with outside investments; that those firms will want to take a heavy hand in controlling the production and strategic decisions of those investments. And public perception only worsens when the investments are in projects that are seen as strategic investments — think critical infrastructure or national security — rather than those that are "simply commercial."

items: Carney's pitch to unlock trillions in global investment
From pipelines to railways and AI: Ottawa pitches 167 projects ahead of Carney's investment summit

blocks.text: But Hejazi says the government can put terms in place that maintain Canada's sovereignty in any potential deal. There's also no evidence to suggest outside companies are more likely to evade regulations, he says, and Canada has strong laws and institutions to combat that if it were to become an issue.

Plus, he says Canada doesn't have the funds to build all of these big-ticket projects on its own. And especially in the current moment — when Canada's relationship with its largest trading partner is so injured — Hejazi says the need for forging new relationships abroad is obvious.
"We need to broaden our global footprint," he said.
But, "at the same time, we do want Canadians to feel that our sovereignty is not being taken by other countries."

He says if any deals are reached because of the summit, the government will need to be very transparent about the terms of those agreements — explaining why they are beneficial for Canada to prevent that skepticism.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Amid Trump trade war, Canada's exports to China up 30% in first half of 2026
articles.summary: The Canada-China Business Council and the University of Alberta's China Institute have crunched the trade data between Canada and China for the first half of 2026, and it shows Canadian exports to…

image.caption: A tanker is pictured in Burrard Inlet, with Stanley Park in the background, near Vancouver on April 20, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Canadian exports to China rocketed by 30 per cent in the first half of 2026, with overall trade up 3.6 per cent year over year, according to Statistics Canada data analyzed by researchers.

The numbers, part of a new report published by the Canada China Business Council and the University of Alberta’s China Institute, appear to reflect the re-engagement between the two countries, which is part of Canada's attempt to diversify its economy amid deteriorating relations with the U.S.
Overall trade in consumer goods between Canada and China totalled $66.6 billion in the first half of 2026, up 3.6 per cent, while exports increased 30 per cent to $21.74 billion year over year.

Energy and minerals dominated, making up 58.4 per cent of all domestic exports to China in that time period, with energy (largely crude oil and liquified propane) alone growing by 81.8 per cent. Metal ores and non-metallic mineral exports (including copper ore) rose 29 per cent.

items: How Canada’s imports and exports have changed since Trump

blocks.text: "This is a record for our first half of the year exports to China," said Bijan Ahmadi, executive director of the Canada China Business Council.
While there has long been trade between the countries — even through the geopolitical tensions of the last few years — the recent jump is likely a result of a confluence of factors.
Geopolitics and Trump
Diplomatic and economic ties between Canada and China are warming up after years of tension over Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou's arrest on a U.S. extradition warrant in 2018.

And as the latest Canada-U.S. trade escalation threatens to widen the rift between Ottawa and Washington indefinitely, Prime Minister Mark Carney has reiterated Canada’s intention to strike new trade deals with other countries and become less reliant on the U.S.

"We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," Carney said in a video address earlier this month, hours after Canada's retaliatory tariffs against billions in U.S. goods took effect. "That pivot will come at a cost. There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still."
Incidentally, the Trans Mountain Pipeline reached 97 per cent capacity in June, substantially increasing Asia’s access to Western Canadian crude oil.

Also aiding the increase in oil exports is the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which disrupted shipments through the vital Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices higher and spurring customers to turn to producers like Canada.
There’s also no country that can replace China’s buying power.
"There is a noted complementarity in our trade ... despite some very significant tensions," said Anton Malkin, head of research at the University of Alberta's China Institute.
In fact, Mark Maki, CEO of Trans Mountain, recently projected that Asia would buy 70 per cent of Canada’s oil by 2028.
"As we expand, I expect most of that expansion will be directed towards Asia," Maki told Reuters on the sidelines of the APPEC industry meeting in Singapore in early September.
Trade truce

The first half of 2026 marked what could be described as a seismic shift in bilateral relations. Carney struck a deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping to allow tens of thousands of Chinese EVs into the domestic market (so far, 15,603 have entered) in exchange for Beijing suspending some tariffs on Canadian agricultural products like canola meal and peas, and reduced tariffs on canola seed.
"We actually saw almost an immediate upswing in price," said Andre Harpe, chair of the Canadian Canola Growers Association and a canola farmer near Grand Prairie, Alta.
Harpe said farmers were selling their canola seed as low as $12 a bushel during the tariff dispute with China. Now, prices have rebounded to $17 a bushel.
Alberta and British Columbia were responsible for the largest export gains, thanks to energy, minerals, forestry and agriculture.
Canada's largest port, in Vancouver, handles about 16 per cent of the country's merchandise trade. A third of it goes to or comes from China, and officials say that's increasing.

"The sentiment that might have existed some time ago, about the inability to get our act together, so to speak, seems to be changing," said Peter Xotta, president and CEO of the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority.
Imports down

While overall trade increased, the breakdown is vastly different when looking at the import numbers, which are down 5.8 per cent year over year, despite China still being Canada's second-largest source of imports.
This dip reduced Canada’s trade deficit with China by 25 per cent, but Malkin says this is in part fuelled by a shift of "certain types of manufacturing outside of China," like Vietnam.
"It’s a bit early, but it’s something worth keeping an eye on," he said.
Fact check: Are only Canada and China retaliating against U.S. tariffs?

Ontario accounted for the largest import decline, which meant fewer purchases of portable computers and video game consoles, which outweighed gains made in lithium-ion batteries and electric vehicles.
Despite the overall gains, the report authors note "agricultural performance improved only modestly," growing 1.9 per cent.
While canola seed, pea and beef exports rose, lobster did not rebound, instead declining by 28 per cent.
"We're a big exporter of lobsters, but we're not the only place where [China] can get lobsters," said Malkin.
Diversify and fortify

Harpe says despite the relief to their bottom lines, farmers are hoping to sell more domestically, to reduce reliance on a single trading partner, especially since the tariff suspension and reductions with China will so far only last until the end of the year.

The authors of the new trade report say Canadian exports to China are still below those to the United Kingdom and European Union, and are not indicative of "uniform improvement" across industries but rather a limited group of commodities.

To Ahmadi, there is room to grow engagement with the Asia-Pacific region, as it represents "significant growing markets," with China alone representing almost half of the market opportunities for businesses.
He says numbers from the end of the year will provide a fuller picture.

If the numbers from the first half of the year are any indication, though, Ahmadi says Canada is "well on track" to achieve the goal set by Ottawa of increasing exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030.
"[We might] even surpass that objective," he said.

articles.title: They lost their savings in an alleged real estate scam. Now, some unexpected relief
articles.summary: A year ago, Janet Campbell thought she’d never get her savings back, after she lost nearly $30,000 in an alleged real estate scam. Now she and several other victims of the alleged scheme have…

image.caption: A 2022 view of construction work on a home in a Vaughan, Ont., subdivision, built by Paradise Developments Inc. Victims of an alleged fraud scheme thought they were buying homes like this one, when in fact they signed agreements and paid deposits to a company with a similar name. (Patrick Morrell/CB

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A year ago, Janet Campbell thought she’d never get her savings back, after she lost nearly $30,000 in an alleged real estate scam. Now she and several other victims of the alleged scheme have received partial reimbursements from Tarion, the organization that administers Ontario’s new home warranty program.
Deposit reimbursement could set precedent for dozens of other victims, says lawyer

A year ago, Janet Campbell thought she'd never get her savings back after losing nearly $30,000 in an alleged real estate scam and spending the rest of her savings on short-term housing when the home she'd planned on didn't materialize.

But in an unexpected development, there's some good news for Campbell and others. The Brampton, Ont., grandmother is one of several victims of the same alleged fraud scheme who have received partial reimbursements from Tarion, the organization that administers Ontario's new home warranty program. In Campbell's case, she was reimbursed $15,000, which she says has helped her to pay off bills that had accumulated.
"I thought that I would just lose everything," Campbell said. "I'm really grateful that I did get some money back."
Campbell's lawyer, Andrew Ballantyne, calls the Tarion decisions "a huge win," and says the development could set a precedent for dozens of other fraud victims.
Tarion is a non-profit organization created by the provincial government that backstops warranty coverage provided by builders for all new homes in Ontario.
Alleged fraud scheme dates back several years

CBC Toronto first reported on the alleged fraud scheme, which primarily targeting members of Toronto's Black community, four years ago. It involved Moiz Kunwar allegedly taking deposits for pre-construction homes he did not have the right to sell and that were being built by unrelated, legitimate developers.
In some cases, buyers lost their life savings on homes that never materialized.
"These aren't wealthy investors who have lost a deposit on their 13th property. These are everyday people who had a dream of owning a home," Ballantyne said.
Kunwar, 29, is now facing numerous fraud charges, which are still before the courts, along with civil lawsuits.

In a statement of defence filed last year in one of the civil claims against him, Kunwar denied all allegations of fraud and denied ever representing himself as a real estate investor, broker, developer or mortgage lender.
Tarion reimburses 7 buyers more than $300,000
That civil lawsuit involves Campbell and six other complainants, who are represented by Ballantyne.

Following a CBC story last year, Ballantyne said he received calls from more than 100 additional buyers who say they were duped by the same scheme. He said he also heard from Tarion's chief operating officer, who suggested there might be grounds for reimbursement claims — something Ballantyne said he hadn't considered.

"I was a little surprised. I didn't think that Tarion would be willing to potentially even consider covering a loss like this," Ballantyne said, since there was never an actual developer involved in the transaction.

Tarion's new home warranty program includes deposit protection. If a builder goes bankrupt or fundamentally breaches a purchase agreement, the buyer's deposit is protected up to certain limits — 10 per cent of the purchase price for homes over $600,000, up to a maximum of $100,000.

After speaking with Tarion, Ballantyne submitted claims on behalf of 12 of his clients, seeking more than $500,000 in reimbursement. So far seven of the claims, including Campbell's, have been approved, four have been denied and one is still pending. The approved payouts total more than $300,000.

items: Is a GTA real estate deal that sounds like paradise too good to be true?
Brampton man facing fraud charge, 2 lawsuits as alleged real estate deposit scam collapses
Dozens more alleged victims come forward as Brampton man accused in real estate fraud faces new charges

blocks.text: The decision letter for Campbell's claim finds that she entered into a home purchase agreement with a vendor, the home was not delivered and she did not receive a deposit refund. Tarion found she therefore met the criteria for deposit protection, despite the fact that the vendor — Paradise Development Homes Limited — is not legally entitled to build homes in Ontario.
Tarion declined CBC Toronto's request for an interview. In an emailed statement, spokesperson Andrew Donnachie called the case "very unusual."
"In evaluating any claim submitted to Tarion, we have to look at the specific details and the requirements under the Ontario New Home Warranties Plan Act," Donnachie said.
He also said the case "highlights the importance of new home purchasers making sure that they are dealing with a licensed builder who has been approved to sell homes."

Earlier this year, Tarion launched a program aimed at catching illegal actors sooner. Buyers are now required to register their purchase with Tarion within 45 days of signing an agreement of purchase and sale.
Buyers who don't register with Tarion will still qualify for coverage, but through a separate fund capped at $15 million annually.
Lawyer to appeal denied claims
Ballantyne says the Tarion reimbursements for his seven clients offer hope to dozens of other affected buyers, but he hopes to expand the precedent further.

One of his clients' denied claims, reviewed by CBC Toronto, indicates that the deposit was paid in two parts — directly to Moiz Kunwar and directly to a numbered company — neither of which matches the name of the vendor on the agreement of purchase and sale.

Ballantyne says payment "irregularities" are a recurring issue for many of the alleged fraud victims. He estimates about half of the more than 100 purchasers he's in touch with made payments to a third party and therefore would likely also see their claims denied.
Ballantyne says he plans to appeal at least three of the denied claims at the Licence Appeal Tribunal, arguing Kunwar and the fraudulent companies he allegedly represented are one and the same.

"It seems obvious to me that there's a clear link between these entities. And it seems to me the result of sticking to this rigid, narrow interpretation of what the vendor is, is going to lead to half of the people not being able to receive their reimbursement," Ballantyne said.
He estimates the lost deposits from the buyers he's in contact with total at least $4 million.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah MacMillan is a journalist with CBC Toronto. She previously reported in Sudbury, Ont., and Prince Edward Island. You can contact her at sarah.macmillan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: This Afghan says Canada is abandoning her in a country where it feels like it's a 'mistake' to be a woman
articles.summary: An Afghan woman who hopes to make it to Canada describes worsening conditions for women living under Taliban rule.

image.caption: An Afghan woman and a girl walk to a primary school in Kabul on Aug. 9, 2022. (AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: "They make you feel that it is a mistake to be a woman in Afghanistan."
Those are the words of a young woman in Kabul describing life in the Afghan capital five years after the chaotic exit of U.S.-led NATO troops made way for the return of Taliban rule in August 2021.
Since then, under the fundamentalist dictates of the self-declared Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, roughly 22 million women and girls have witnessed what rights they did enjoy stripped away.
"It started with a ban on schools, then going to markets, going to travel, then jobs, universities," said the woman. "[It feels] like you have to get permission to breathe even."
To protect her from any potential repercussions from this interview or for her previous work for Canadian-funded projects in Afghanistan, I will refer to her as X.
Over the past five years, the Taliban have issued dozens of edicts aimed at suppressing women.

They are forbidden from being outside without a male guardian, from holding most jobs and studying beyond primary school. They're not allowed to visit parks or playgrounds or gyms or salons or even raise their voices in public.

A report this summer by UN Women, the UN body dedicated to gender equality, found that half of Afghan women surveyed were only leaving their homes once or twice a month "because of severe restrictions on their movement and access to public spaces."
"[It's] like you're living at home [and] there are zombies outside," said X. "If we go outside, there are so many people that can attack us.

"They can arrest us with just not wearing a proper hijab. If I go like this outside, they will not allow me for one second," she said, referring to the light headscarf she was wearing during our video call, her face exposed.
Pain and disappointment
It is a suffocating reality for all Afghan women, but for X it has an added layer of pain and disappointment.

Before the Western exodus from Afghanistan, she worked for aid organizations funded by Global Affairs Canada (GAC), implementing Ottawa's Afghanistan objectives, which included the empowerment of women and girls.
Hers was a public-facing role in the community.

That work put her at risk when the Taliban took over. The work also meant she was entitled to apply for the Special Immigration Measures Program (SIMs) for Afghans who assisted the government of Canada introduced in July 2021, which she did, along with thousands of others.
A spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said Friday that the country has welcomed 65,540 Afghans under all immigration streams, including the SIMs program, since August 2021.
Within those numbers, Canada has approved 16,560 applications out of 20,605 received for the SIMs program, resulting in 16,525 arrivals to Canada, the spokesperson said.
One of the requirements was an endorsement by GAC or the Department of National Defence stating that the individual in question had an "enduring relationship with Canada."
X was given that endorsement.
'Full endorsement of GAC'
"I can assure you that your application has been deemed eligible and referred to the relevant authorities at IRCC," a development officer from GAC's Afghanistan program wrote to her.
"I can personally confirm that your case has been given the full endorsement of GAC."
Despite that, X was never issued an invitation to formally apply to the program from IRCC.
She was still waiting for that invitation in the fall of 2023 when I first interviewed her remotely for a story about life under the Taliban.
She had received a reply of receipt to her request for the SIMs program on Aug. 6, 2021, as the Taliban advanced on Kabul.

A year later, after having enquired to the status of her SIMs application more than once, she received a response telling her that because she had not been issued an invitation to apply by IRCC, her application had been cancelled.
My own inquiries to GAC over her situation and the system in general went unanswered.
Where did the applications go?
X wasn't alone.
In 2022, the NDP's immigration critic at the time, MP Jenny Kwan, alleged that the government had lost 2,900 SIMs applications.
There is also anecdotal evidence of others having their applications disappear into a bureaucratic black hole.
One retired Canadian colonel seeking to assist local support staff for the Canadian Armed Forces in Afghanistan has said applications were lost or unacknowledged in an overwhelmed IRCC system.
"I really didn't think that I will have been left behind," X said in our recent conversation. "I had expectations that the government of Canada would have helped me."
The sense of abandonment adds to the weight she and many other Afghans feel toward the outside world after the collapse of the Western-backed government in Kabul.
For X, it led to depression, with sleep a symptom of, and a coping mechanism for, that depression.
The shock of seeing her future so abruptly stunted and the value of her past accomplishments erased is still with her.
"The mental wellness is a joke [in Afghanistan]," she said. "I do not only think about myself. I think about every girl who is staying at home right now."
A few connections to the outside world
X lives a more privileged life than many Afghans. Her family can afford the internet, which offers at least a window on the outside world. And she has continued to study statistics online.
She lives with elderly parents and a sister but has a married sister living in the U.S. and a brother in Canada who X says assumed she would be able to join him through the SIMs program.
Her father's poor health has meant he is rarely able to act as guardian or mahram for the women in the household when they need or want to go out.
Oppression of Afghan women only growing 5 years after Taliban takeover
She cites that as one reason for accepting a marriage proposal, a decision she says she made without any pressure from her parents.
"I have always considered myself [to be] strong.

"But when the outside world is cruel to you and they do not accept your existence, and they might even respect an animal rather than a woman … you get this feeling of at least having a man by your side you at least can go somewhere without those fears and you have at least someone to depend on."
Looking for more security

Some of the most recent Taliban decrees "place husbands in a position of legal authority over their wives and limiting women's ability to seek justice," according to the UN Women report. And they "implicitly permit" child marriage and only criminalize violence against women within a marriage when it results in "severe visible physical injuries."
X hopes her decision to marry will offer her family more security.
"I was saying OK, at least he will be like a son to this family. Because our brother is not here, he will support us."
It doesn't mean she has given up on her hope of immigrating to Canada.
The government of Canada's website says that while all spots for the SIMs program have been filled, existing applications will continue to be processed.
Whether X's name is among them is anybody's guess.

items: Retired major calls on Ottawa to keep promise and bring Afghan man to safety in N.L.
Five years after Kabul fell, the reckoning over Afghanistan is far from over

blocks.text: Over the summer, X wrote a letter to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab.

"Today, women in Afghanistan are facing severe restrictions, isolation and danger," it said. "Every day feels smaller, darker and more uncertain. For someone like me who believed in education, equality and humanitarian work, the risk is not abstract. It is real and immediate.
"I respectfully ask you to reconsider my case and help ensure that those who served alongside Canadian initiatives are not left behind," she wrote.
"Please do not let my story end in silence."

articles.title: They came to Canada for safety. Now they’re suspected of supporting the regime they fled
articles.summary: Hundreds of permanent resident applicants received letters from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada in August, advocates say. The letters state concerns the applicants could be members of…

image.caption: Farzin Jafari finished two years of mandatory military service with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2011. In August, he received a letter from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada that said his permanent residency application could be denied due to concerns he is still a member. (Is

blocks.text: Farzin Jafari is facing an impossible choice: wait and hope the Canadian government allows him and his family to remain in Canada, or leave his wife and infant daughter in hopes they can stay if he's deemed inadmissible and forced to return to Iran.
“We are hanging from a rope as a family,” he said. “If I leave that rope, open my hand, and fall… at least my family can stay alive.”

Jafari is one of what one advocacy group says is hundreds of permanent residency applicants who received a Procedural Fairness Letter (PFL) from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada in August.

The letters indicated applicants may be inadmissible to Canada because of their connection to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and would need to prove otherwise. The Canadian government listed the IRGC as a terrorist organization in 2024.

“I am therefore concerned that you served in the IRGC and that you may be inadmissible to Canada per paragraph 34(1)(f) for being a member of an organization … engaging in terrorism,” the letter said.
Jafari said he didn’t have a choice where he served.
“You can't say, ‘I don't want this,’” Jafari said.
I'm not IRGC. I'm a victim of IRGC.- Farzin Jafari

Iran's Revolutionary Guards are a branch of the Iranian military with broad powers that answers directly to the country’s supreme leader. All Iranian men over the age of 18 are required to complete compulsory military service.
Proof of service is required to work or obtain a passport and conscripts have no say in the branch they serve under.
“If you don't participate in that compulsory period, you can't have your basic civil rights,” Jafari said. “They are holding you hostage in the country until you pass this period.”
If a citizen says they don’t want to serve, they risk being jailed by the Iranian government.
Iranian told he may have to leave Canada over past IRGC service
IRGC deemed a terrorist organization
Jafari completed his mandatory military service in 2011. CBC News has seen his completion card, a document provided by the Iranian military that shows he finished compulsory service.
He described his work as administrative, recording licence plates.
After finishing, he worked privately as a software engineer in Iran before moving to Canada in 2021 to start a family.

His wife had been briefly detained by Iranian morality police and he said they feared for their safety. He has spent much of his free time in Canada protesting the Iranian government and calling for the IRGC’s designation as a terrorist entity.
Jafari and his wife submitted their permanent residency applications in the winter of 2024.

That summer the Canadian government listed the IRGC as a terrorist organization and said the IRGC had provided support to other terror groups including Hezbollah, Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Taliban.
In January 2020, the IRGC shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight PS752 above the skies of Tehran and killed 175 passengers, including 55 Canadian citizens and 30 permanent residents.

Justice Minister Arif Virani said while making the designation on June 19, 2024, the government was concerned about the impact of the listing on those conscripted into the IRGC, but was "careful and measured" in its approach.
"If an individual was conscripted at one point in time and no longer serves with the IRGC, that would affect the analysis," he said at the time.
Canada designates Iran's Revolutionary Guard a terrorist entity
So when Jafari and his wife received PFLs because of his mandatory service, he was shocked.
“I'm not IRGC. I'm a victim of IRGC,” he said.
‘Hundreds’ of letters sent
Hundreds of applicants received similar letters on Aug. 6 and 7, according to Nahid Rahmati, a representative of the Unheard Conscripts Advocacy Network.
The group seeks to represent people conscripted to the IRGC and advocate for them within the Canadian immigration system.
Rahmati said she’s never seen anyone receive a PFL and be accepted into Canada.
“I have seen lots of cases that have been rejected,” she said. “They got the PFL and they got rejected.”
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said in a statement it could not confirm the number of letters sent to permanent residency applicants in relation to potential IRGC ties.

items: Are Iranian 'sleeper cells' a threat to Canadians? Here’s what intelligence experts say
Iranian dissidents in Canada say they're being watched and under threat from the regime in Iran

blocks.text: CBC News spoke with several recipients of the letters, many of whom declined to speak on the record for fear of retribution from the government of Iran.
Letters part of ‘normal’ process

In a statement, Canada's immigration and citizenship department said the listing of the guard as a terrorist entity prompts an “assessment of inadmissibility concerns where applications indicate a connection to the IRGC.”
“This is a normal part of applying Canada’s immigration law and does not mean that every person who served in the IRGC is automatically inadmissible."

Conscripts said it is difficult to prove they did not participate in the IRGC after their mandatory service ended. The IRGC does not keep a list of people who left, according to Hossein Raeesi, a criminal and human rights lawyer who practiced in Iran for two decades.
“Someone who served compulsory military service with the IRGC is not considered as a member of the IRGC,” he said.
CBC News asked the Canadian government which documents it would accept as proof that an applicant was not a member of the IRGC beyond mandatory service.
“There is no single prescribed set of documents that applies to every case,” the agency said in a statement.
Conscripts served under duress, lawyer says
Many of the conscripts served under duress, according to Arghavan Gerami, an immigration lawyer based in Ottawa.
Two of her current clients have received PFLs and she worries Canada is expecting them to prove they tried to resist conscription.
“What are we telling them to do? ‘Say no, stand up to the regime?’” she said. “This is a country that doesn't respect the rule of law. We've seen them kill and shoot civilians and protesters.”
“These people have families and wives. We're asking them to stand up to that regime, say no to something that's mandatory and essentially put themselves in harm's way.”
She added it’s important to deny entry to high-ranking IRGC officials and those who volunteered for service willingly.
“The focus should be [on] individuals that we know are in Canada who are really the key culprits.”
Living in uncertainty
Canada has temporarily paused the removal of inadmissible individuals to Iran due to concerns for civilian safety amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
If Jafari is deemed inadmissible, he and his wife could be removed from Canada when the pause ends — and forced to take their infant daughter to Iran with them.
For now, all Jafari can do is wait.
“It’s a very desperate situation,” he said.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Ill-gotten wealth, unexplained wealth, hidden wealth
articles.summary: During the 24th day of Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial, House panel prosecution witness and former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang tackled ill-gotten wealth,…

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 3:54pm

During the 24th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, House panel prosecution witness and former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang tackled ill-gotten wealth, unexplained wealth, and hidden wealth.
What are the differences between the three?
Unexplained wealth

Republic Act (RA) 1379 or the Unexplained Wealth Act describes unexplained wealth as property and/or money acquired by an official during his incumbency, whether in his name or in the name of other persons, that is manifestly out of proportion to his salary and to his other lawful income.
Section 2 of the law states that the said property shall be presumed “prima facie” to have been unlawfully acquired.
Cabotaje-Tang said prima facie translates to “on its face.”

“Ang ibig sabihin niyan kapag napakita na yung isang official ay nag acquire ng property that is groslly or manifestly disproportionate to his salary, lawful income, and income from lawfully acquired properties, ito ay pinapalagay na unlawfully acquired,” she said.

(It means that once it is shown that an official acquired property that is grossly or manifestly disproportionate to his salary, lawful income, and income from lawfully acquired properties, it is presumed to have been unlawfully acquired.)
She clarified that this did not mean mean an official is immediately guilty.
Cabotaje-Tang said if the official can satisfactorily explain that the properties were acquired lawfully, then the validity of the presumption will be gone.
Meanwhile, Section 8 of RA 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act Section states that if an official is found to have unexplained wealth, this shall be ground for dismissal or removal.

Further, it states that properties in the name of the spouse and unmarried children of the public official may be taken into consideration, whether their acquisition through legitimate means cannot be satisfactorily shown.
Aside from this, bank deposits may also be taken into consideration.
Ill-gotten wealth

Executive Order (EO) No. 1 defined ill-gotten wealth as “any asset, property, business enterprise or material possession of persons within the purview of EO Nos. 1 and 2, acquired by them directly, or indirectly, thru dummies, nominees, agents, subordinates, and/or business associates through the following:

items: Through misappropriations, conversion, misuse or malversation of public funds or raids on the public treasury;

Through the receipt, directly or indirectly, of any commission, gift, share, percentage, kickbacks or any other form of pecuniary benefit from any person and/or entity in connection with any government contract or project or by reason of the office or position of the official concerned;
By the illegal or fraudulent conveyance or disposition of assets belonging to the government or any of its subdivisions, agencies or instrumentalities or government-owned or controlled corporations;
By obtaining, receiving or accepting directly or indirectly any shares of stock, equity or any other form of interest or participation in any business enterprise or undertaking;

Through the establishment of agricultural, industrial or commercial monopolies or other combination and/or by the issuance, promulgation and/or implementation of decrees and orders intended to benefit particular persons or special interests; and
By taking undue advantage of official position, authority, relationship or influence for personal gain or benefit.

blocks.text: Under the EO, ill-gotten wealth may be sequestered by the state.
Hidden wealth
Meanwhile, Cabotaje-Tang explained that a hidden wealth is a property owned by a public official but is registered under another individual.
“For example, a public officer owns a property but that property is registered in the name of another person,” she said.
According to Cabotaje-Tang, there are stricter prohibitions for the president, the vice president, cabinet secretaries, undersecretaries, and assistant secretaries.
She said this is because “there is greater possibility of abuse in their office given their positions.”
Cabotaje-Tang testified on Article 2, which refers to unexplained wealth. — RSJ, GMA News

image.caption: Iran is looking beyond its southern ports as it seeks alternative routes for trade and importsImage: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Can land corridors offset the impact of the maritime blockade on Iran? The US-led maritime blockade targeting Iranian ports has severely disrupted trade through its southern ports, but it is also accelerating a strategy Tehran had discussed for years: moving more commerce through northern ports, railways and land corridors.

Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh, visiting Moscow for talks with Russian officials, said Iran should activate its northern borders and shift a significant share of imports and exports away from the country's southern maritime routes.

The idea is straightforward. Iran has seven land neighbors, access to the Caspian Sea and several routes linking it to Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and the Caucasus. In theory, that gives Tehran more options than a country dependent on a single maritime gateway.
The question is whether those routes have enough capacity to replace what is being lost at sea.

blocks.caption: Iran's southern ports, like the Port of Bandar Abbas shown here, have traditionally handled the bulk of the country's maritime tradeImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Northern routes offer room to expand
Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, told DW that Iran does have unused capacity.
"Iran has more room to maneuver than its dependence on southern ports might suggest,” he said.

Iranian authorities said in late 2025 that the country's northern ports had more than 30 million tons of nominal annual capacity, with less than one-third in use. That suggests room for more grain, food and general cargo through the Caspian Sea.
Turkey provides another route toward Europe. Rail freight between Iran and Turkey depends partly on train ferries across Lake Van, which carried about 477,000 tons in 2024.

To the northeast, Sarakhs and Incheh Borun connect Iran through Turkmenistan toward Central Asia, Russia and potentially China. To the northwest, Astara is part of the International North-South Transport Corridor linking Iran to Azerbaijan and Russia, he said.

The Astara freight terminal is designed for 3.5 to 4 million tons a year, but handled only about 345,000 tons in the first five months of 2026. The unfinished Rasht-Astara rail link remains an important bottleneck.
For specific goods, these routes matter. Grain from Russia and Kazakhstan, medicines, industrial inputs and regional trade can be redirected more easily than crude oil.

blocks.caption: Freight trains are a key part of Iran's efforts to expand trade through overland routes Image: Amir/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volume is the main obstacle

Jafar Ghaderi, a member of Iranian parliament's Economic Commission, recently said that 83% of what he described as Iran's 210 million tons of imports had traditionally moved through southern maritime borders, a tremendous volume of goods.
"Whenever we are under a maritime blockade, we face problems," hhe said. "How much capacity do our eastern, western and northern corridors actually have?"

The cost difference is also large. Majidreza Hariri, head of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce, said shipping one container from China to Iran through southern ports costs about $3,000 (€2,580), and that moving the same container overland costs roughly $12,000.
With around 2 million containers entering through the south annually, Hariri estimated that a prolonged shift to land routes could add about $18 billion to Iran's trading costs.
Salavati said the physical arithmetic helps explain why.

A 50,000-ton shipload would require around 2,000 truck journeys if each lorry carried 25 tons. Those trucks would then be unavailable for domestic distribution, while longer journeys increase fuel, insurance, warehousing and border costs.
Low-value goods are particularly vulnerable because transport expenses account for a larger share of their final price.

blocks.caption: Maritime cargo volumes are difficult to replicate via rail and road corridorsImage: Rouzbeh Fouladi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Energy is much harder to reroute
Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said Iranian officials are often discussing two different kinds of alternatives.
One involves alternative navigation lanes around Hormuz. The other involves shifting trade toward Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, the Caspian region, Jask and Chabahar.
Neither provides a full substitute for southern energy exports.
A large crude tanker can carry roughly 1.5 to 2 million barrels. Replicating that volume by road would require thousands of tanker trucks.
Rail is more efficient, but still cannot match the cost, speed or scale of maritime transport.
Pakistan can help move imports through Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Iraq can support regional trade and limited fuel flows. Caspian routes can connect Iran to Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.
But none can replace large-scale crude shipments to Asian buyers.
"So the plan is realistic as a resilience strategy, but not as a replacement strategy,” Shokri told DW.
How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz?
Jask pipeline shows both potential and limits
The Goreh-Jask pipeline was built specifically to reduce Iran's dependence on the Strait of Hormuz by moving crude to the Gulf of Oman.
That gives Jask greater strategic importance than most overland corridors.
But Shokri says actual usable capacity has remained far below the project's original ambition.
The lesson is broader: building a pipeline is not the same as creating a functioning export system. Storage, terminals, buyers, insurance, security and financial settlement all have to work together.
Fixed infrastructure also creates new vulnerabilities during wartime.

blocks.caption: Energy infrastructure can improve resilience, but fixed assets such as pipelines also create new vulnerabilities during conflictImage: Ahmad Halabisaz/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: A resilience strategy, not an escape route
Land corridors can help Iran keep essential economic activity alive.
They can move food, medicine, industrial inputs and some regional exports. They can also deepen Iran's economic links with Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq.
If investment continues, the blockade may accelerate infrastructure projects that Tehran had previously treated as long-term opportunities.
But these routes come with higher costs, limited capacity and their own political dependencies.
For Iran, that means the blockade could leave a lasting structural effect by pushing trade away from the south and making northern and overland connections more important.
It does not mean Iran can replace maritime trade.

The corridors can reduce vulnerability, distribute risk and buy time. They cannot reproduce the scale of the Persian Gulf ports and seaborne energy exports on which much of Iran's economy has long depended.

articles.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
articles.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet,…

image.caption: One quarter of Berlin's residents do not have German citizenship and therefore no right to voteImage: Winfried Rothermel/IMAGO

blocks.text: Abdu Taviq, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Taviq is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly annoying at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.
"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to kindergartens and German courses, for example, affect me directly."
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet
Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.
Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's upcoming election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, this will be a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

blocks.caption: Around a third of adults in Stefanie Remlinger's district don't have German nationality Image: Annette Hauschild

blocks.text: Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Taviq is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.
How Berliners are reshaping their city for the future
Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Taviq decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership says it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.
Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.

Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens. (Though that happens to be another one of Taviq's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response.")

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.
More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Taviq, but, in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: AI-linked stocks fall after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development
articles.summary: Shares in tech firms tumble across Asia with Nasdaq also likely to dip later after Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX leaders back call

blocks.text: AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.

Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer of OpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chip makers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.

In Taipei, shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%. Futures for the Nasdaq pointed to a 1.3% drop in the tech-heavy index when the US stock market opens this afternoon.
The sell-off comes after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”.
He said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.

Amodei’s claims have been disputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.
The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support for Amodei’s essay on slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.
Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.

Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world has laws sufficient to contain them.

However, Donald Trump rejected the calls to pace AI development. The US president told reporters over the weekend: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.

“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.”
after newsletter promotion

“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.

“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”
Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.

The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year.
OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 due to safety concerns with the technology.

articles.title: Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank
articles.summary:
Report by Israeli human rights group says systematic and broad assault being waged on conditions required for Palestinians’ existence

Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination”…
articles.byline: Quique Kierszenbaum in Sair, and Peter Beaumont

blocks.text: Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination” of the conditions that sustain Palestinian collective life in the occupied West Bank, according to a major report published by the human rights group B’Tselem.

The Israeli organisation’s hard-hitting report, shared with the Guardian in advance of publication, says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank”, including “the ability to get to work, take children to school or university, receive medical treatment or municipal services, meet family and friends, cultivate land or go on vacation … routine activities that make up human life”.

According to B’Tselem, the assault on Palestinians is “governed by a coherent organising logic” and comprises five “interwoven domains of action”: violence and intimidation, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.

The publication of the Elimination Project, B’Tselem’s most comprehensive piece of work on the West Bank since its launch in 1989, comes less than a week after the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, accused settler terrorists, supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, of committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, in the UK’s starkest condemnation of Israel since the foundation of the state.
1,107Number of Palestinians killed by Israel in the West Bank since October 2023

By looking more broadly at the conditions required for Palestinians’ collective existence, however, the B’Tselem report goes further still. It says various arms of the Israeli state – led by Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister with broad powers over civilian matters in the West Bank – are seeking to “create a reality in which millions of Palestinians live in constant fear of Israeli military and civilian violence”.

“Palestinian communities are being pushed out in an accelerating process of ethnic cleansing, while an ever-expanding Israeli presence is being established in their place in the form of settlements, outposts, farms and Jewish-only civilian infrastructure,” the report says. “Elimination in this context means sustained harm to the conditions that enable Palestinians to exist as a people with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history, and a social and political horizon.

“It is an ongoing political project that seeks to re-organise space and the conditions of life so that Jewish presence becomes contiguous, institutionalised and permanent, while Palestinian existence becomes fragmented, vulnerable and dependent.”
One of the most obvious aspects of this fragmentation is the closure of roads and villages to Palestinian passage, and the abandonment of Palestinian homes under relentless pressure.

On a recent afternoon outside the village of Sair, Haytham Adnan Murad, 49, was returning from a hospital appointment in Hebron with his 12-year-old daughter, Balqis, who is unable to walk because of recent surgery. A gate to the road accessing his village, open in the morning, had been closed by the Israeli army, forcing Murad to get out of the taxi he was travelling in with his daughter and carry her around the roadblock.

blocks.caption: Haytham Adnan Murad carrying his daughter, Balqis, around an Israeli roadblock. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “When we left, the gate was open. Now it’s closed, but this is daily life,” he said. “In the morning, things are different from the afternoon. There’s no dignity in this.”

The authors of the report link the acceleration of the Israeli assault on life in the West Bank to the period after the Hamas attack on southern Israeli communities on 7 October 2023. However, they argue that the underlying motivating ideology predates this period.

In particular they point to a document known as the Decisive Plan, published by Smotrich in 2017, before he became a minister, which they describe as the “key document for understanding Israeli action in the West Bank.”
64 Number of entire communities forcibly displaced in the West Bank since October 2023

B’Tselem says the plan gave Palestinians three options: “Live under Jewish supremacy while relinquishing their national claims, leave the territory, or face violent suppression by the Israeli military if they resist”. It has been translated, the report adds, “into policy, budgets, powers and practices exercised by different arms of the state” with “unprecedented speed and openness”.
As such, the report goes on, settler violence is no longer “operating only as private violence or a breach of public order” but as part of a “broader system of control”.
“It is sometimes carried out alongside soldiers, with the backing of security forces, using weapons, equipment and infrastructure supplied by the state, and with almost complete impunity.”

Beyond the already well-documented incidents of escalating settler violence, the report highlights other corrosive aspects of the tightening Israeli grip on the West Bank, including devastating economic restrictions, and impacts on education and culture.
31.3%Unemployment rate in the West Bank in 2024, up from 13.1% in 2022

Israel, it says, has enacted a systematic policy of “full economic strangulation” since 2023, which has denied livelihood opportunities, destroyed civilian and agricultural infrastructure, tightened control over resources and the banking system, and undermined the ability of public institutions to provide basic services.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian shepherd from the hamlet of Anizan, where residents have been repeatedly driven out of their homes by settlers. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Smotrich said in September 2025 he would employ every means possible “to prevent the danger of a Palestinian state, including bringing about the collapse of the Palestinian Authority … through economic strangulation”.

Mass work permit revocations have left workers and their families without a stable income. This is reflected in data from the West Bank cited in the report. The unemployment rate, for instance, rose from 13.1% in 2022 to 31.3% in 2024, and in 2025, nearly half of all young people were neither employed nor enrolled in education or vocational training.
The UN has estimated that in 2024, 700,000 Palestinians in the West Bank needed assistance to buy food, a 17% increase from the previous year.

Since October 2023, Israel has also intensified attacks on various Palestinian organisations and associations in the West Bank. Grassroots and community groups, as well as organisations that protect workers, people in need and children, have faced frequent raids on their offices, forced closure, systematic harassment and the arrest of employees, volunteers and activists without cause.
Cogat, the Israeli military unit responsible for overseeing civilian policy in the West Bank and Gaza, has been approached for comment.
8 to 20%Proportion of West Bank schools closed in the 2023-24 academic year

In an interview conducted to coincide with the report’s publication, Kareem Jubran, the head of B’Tselem’s field research on the West Bank, said: “What we uncovered is that these are not separate incidents. All the disparate elements have one character, one goal. When you look at the picture from above, it leads to one conclusion: that the main goal is to eliminate Palestinians as a collective.”

blocks.caption: The remnants of the Palestinian shepherds’ village of al-Qabun after settler violence forced its inhabitants to leave. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Yuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem, said: “What we are saying in the report is that this is ongoing. The project was there before, but now we are in a new phase.

“It started at the end of 2022, with the change of the government [to a right-far right coalition], and we saw another marked escalation after October 2023. What we are talking about is an attack on Palestinian life in the West Bank that changed in scale. It’s as much a quantitative element that has changed, making the West Bank more and more unlivable for many Palestinians.”

Novak described Smotrich’s plan from 2017 as the “blueprint”. “It shows the ideological and the operational way to get to what we are calling an elimination,” he said. “And he calls it victory by settlement. To win in a very final way so that nothing [such as a Palestinian state] can happen afterwards.”
All data and figures provided by B’Tselem

articles.title: Bali police investigate after Australian man and children found dead in home
articles.summary: Police were called after the man's wife became concerned and asked neighbours to check on her family.

blocks.text: Police in Bali are investigating after the bodies of an Australian man and his two children were found dead in their bungalow in a popular tourist area.
Damien John Shaw, 56, and his two children, a boy aged six and a girl aged four, were found dead in their home in Kuta on Sunday.
Police said neighbours had checked in on the family after a call from the man's wife, who had become concerned after a phone call with her husband. She was not in Bali at the time.

Australian media reported that police were treating the case as a suspected murder-suicide. Police told the BBC they had not yet determined the cause or manner of death and that further examinations would be carried out.
Police said the man's wife had called a neighbour after hearing one of her children crying while on the phone to her husband. She was subsequently unable to contact him again.
His wife had reportedly travelled to the capital Jakarta in the previous days.

Police said that the neighbour, accompanied by other local residents, had then forced their way into the property after there was no response to their knocks. The three victims were discovered inside.
Police said Shaw was originally from Fremantle in Western Australia. Roger Cook, the state's premier, described the news as a "very confronting situation".
"This is a very sad situation; our hearts go out to everyone involved. We hope we can get to the bottom of what's gone on as soon as possible," he added.
