articles.title: Tang: Cash cannot be lumped with other properties in SALN
articles.summary: Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang on Monday said that cash on hand and cash in bank of government officials must be separately declared in the Statement of Assets,…

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 2:53pm

Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang on Monday said that cash on hand and cash in bank of government officials must be separately declared in the Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and must not be lumped together with other properties.

Tang said this on the 24th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte upon the interjection of Senator-Judge Joel Villanueva, who asked about the lumping of cash in other assets in the SALN.
“Well, under [Republic Act No.] 6713, ‘yung cash on hand and cash in bank, they must be specifically declared in the SALN. Hindi pwedeng i-lump ‘yun sa ibang other personal properties,” Tang said.
(Well, under RA 6713, the cash on hand and cash in bank must be specifically declared in the SALN. It cannot be lumped with other personal properties.)
Villanueva pressed Tang, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel, if she would consider the lumping in of cash with other assets an “unusual practice.”
“I will not consider it unusual, but it is against the provision of Section 8 of RA 6713,” she said.

“Pero again, doon kasi po sa kaso ni Carlos vs. Executive Secretary, meron po tayong tinatawag na review and compliance procedure under Section 10 of 6713 na binibigyan ng pagkakataon actually ‘yung public official para ayusin kung meron,” she added.

(But then again, in the case of Carlos vs. Executive Secretary, there is what we call a review and compliance procedure under Section 10 of Republic Act No. 6713, which actually gives the public official the opportunity to take the necessary corrective action.)
To recall, the absence of Duterte’s cash in bank on her SALN declarations from 2019 to 2024 was flagged during the House justice committee hearing on the impeachment complaints against her.

Duterte and her husband, Atty. Manases "Mans" Carpio reportedly had a total net worth of P55 million in 2019. It grew to P56 million in 2020; P65 million in 2021; P71 million in 2022; P77 million in 2023; P88 million in 2024; and sans cash on hand and deposits.

Atty. Michael Poa, spokesperson for the Vice President’s defense team, explained that Duterte has no cash on hand declared in her official SALN since 2019 because it was "lumped" under the “others” line item.
Poa said that Duterte’s cash in bank and even jewelry were also “lumped” all together under that specific line item. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Pauline Hanson’s comments about Indigenous Australians condemned as ‘nasty’ and ‘derogatory’
articles.summary: Indigenous senators have criticised One Nation leader saying the comments showed ‘wilful ignorance’

blocks.text: Federal parliamentarians from across the political spectrum have joined in condemning resurfaced comments by Pauline Hanson as “nasty” and “derogatory”, after she labelled Indigenous Australians the “most primitive race on Earth”.

The Indigenous affairs minister, Malarndirri McCarthy, a Yanyuwa and Garrwa woman, described the One Nation senator’s comments as “totally outrageous” while her opposition counterpart, Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, said Hanson’s comments showed “wilful ignorance” and had “dragged the conversation into appalling territory”.

Meanwhile, the independent senator Lidia Thorpe urged the Albanese government to focus on real action, including implementing the national anti-racism framework, warning Hanson won’t stop spreading “nasty, poorly informed and harmful ideas”.
The comments place Hanson once more in the centre of attention, and ire from critics, following a string of high-profile slanging matches.
In a September 2025 podcast, and first reported by News24, Hanson complained about children learning about Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander history.
The 72-year-old One Nation leader, who has a history of making controversial statements about Indigenous Australians, said they were the “most primitive race on earth” and had “achieved nothing”.
On Monday, McCarthy shot back at the comments, instructing Hanson to apologise to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander constituents she represents as a senator for Queensland.
“There is rich history in this country and you only have to travel to places like the Great Barrier Reef, to Cape York, to see incredible cultural significance. Dance, songs and stories,” she said.
“But that’s just one part of Australia. The rest of the country is rich with First Nations culture.”
Price, who was the face of the Indigenous voice to parliament’s no campaign, said she was disappointed by the comments, and was sure it would be condemned by all decent Australians.

“Some of the issues raised by Pauline Hanson are serious debates, many of which I have been very vocal about, but yet again, Senator Hanson has dragged the conversation into appalling territory,” she said.

“Senator Hanson’s statement asking, ‘What the hell have they done in this country?’ is a demonstration of wilful ignorance on her part and reveals her complete failure to understand Australia’s First Peoples.”
Hanson claimed in the podcast that she had asked Price to join One Nation before the 2025 federal election, saying “she’s a better fit” with her party over the Liberals.
after newsletter promotion
Thorpe said most Australians knew the comments were “simply false”.

“For thousands of generations, First Peoples have cared for this continent, developed sophisticated systems of lore, knowledge, agriculture, land management, science and art, and maintained rich living cultures that continue today,” she said.
“First Peoples’ ancient knowledge of this continent is something we want to share with everyone, to bring this country together. But Hanson is only interested in division.
“Before spreading these stereotypes, Hanson should consider the real harm she does to people.
“But I don’t really care about trying to change her mind. We know she won’t change. She will continue to spread nasty, poorly informed and harmful ideas to rally her base and divide this country.”
Thorpe said the federal government could include action to address racism in its recently unveiled digital duty of care plan.
Hanson responded to criticism on social media: “The media is in a tailspin again today about comments made a year ago on this podcast. Have a look. You be the judge.”

articles.title: Canada seeks 'unique alliance' with EU, Carney says
articles.summary: Mark Carney clarified Canada's EU ambitions amid a WSJ report that Ottawa was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc.

image.caption: Canada has already increased its closeness with the EUImage: Andrej Ivanov/AFP

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday said he was pursuing unprecedented closeness with the European Union to reduce its dependence on its economically hostile neighbor, but not a membership with the bloc.
"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival.

"What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — is a unique ​alliance between Canada and the European Union," he said. "We share the same values, we have the same priorities and ​we have very complementary strengths."

Carney's clarification came after a report by the Wall Street Journal claimed he was exploring whether Canada could become an "associate member" of the bloc. The newspaper reported that the EU was open to the idea of granting Canada associate membership — a status it would have to create for the North American nation.
Zelenskyy strengthens defense ties with Canada
Carney's mission EU
The remarks precede the Canadian prime minister's scheduled trip to France this week.
In Strasbourg, France, Carney will become the first head of government to attend the "State of the European Union" address before delivering his own speech at the European Parliament.
His visit is a "tremendous symbol," said Tobias Cremer, a European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a March resolution calling for stronger EU-Canada cooperation.
"Canada has many of the resources that Europe is very much short of, whether it's in terms of energy, whether it's rare earths (and) raw minerals," Cremer said.
Canada is already the first non-EU Nation to join the bloc's defense procurement program, while Carney was involved in Canada joining the Eurovision Song Contest for 2027.
Meanwhile, Montreal is set to host an EU-Canada summit where Carney said discussions will begin on building a "much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership."
Canada's increasing closeness with the EU comes when the country is in the middle of an escalating trade war with its largest trading partner and neighbor, the United States.

articles.title: Germany: Merz's CDU comes out on top in Lower Saxony polls
articles.summary: The Christian Democrats have emerged as the strongest party at local elections in the state of Lower Saxony. The vote was closely watched as an indicator of the strength of the far-right AfD, which…

image.caption: Chancellor Merz's CDU has won local elections in Lower SaxonyImage: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has remained the strongest force at district level in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony following local elections there, preliminary results released on Monday show.

The elections on Sunday received an unusual degree of attention, as they were seen as a gauge of support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) following its landslide win in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last week.
The elections were to choose mayors, district administrations and local councils in the state.
What were the election results in Lower Saxony?

In what will doubtless be a relief for under-pressure Chancellor Friedrich Merz, his CDU came in first with 27.2% of the vote, slightly down on the 31.7% it reached in the last local elections in Lower Saxony in 2021.
The Social Democrats (SPD), who lead a coalition government at state level, were in second place with 24.6% support, a sharp drop from the 30% achieved in 2021.
The AfD followed with 15.9%, more than tripling its result in 2021.
The Greens, who are the junior coalition partners at state level, were on 14.1%, compared with 15.9% in 2021.
The Left party and the Free Democrats (FDP) brought up the tail with 6% and 3.7% respectively.
High turnout in Lower Saxony
Some 6.3 million people were eligible to take part in the elections, which saw a turnout of 64.6%, well up on the 57% participation at the 2021 polls.
Any run-off elections will take place across the state on September 27.

The poll in Lower Saxony was seen not only as a test of public sentiment ahead of state elections next year but also as a barometer of how the AfD is currently faring in western German states, where the far-right party has less support than in the east.
The elections in the state come just a week before the next state polls in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and the city-state of Berlin.
The vote in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will be under especially close scrutiny, with the AfD expected to make strong gains while the CDU is polling at just 7%.

articles.title: ‘Tidal wave’ of Pfas being launched to satisfy AI industry, campaigners warn
articles.summary:
Big manufacturers planning to produce more of the forever chemicals to meet demand from datacentres

Pfas companies are launching a “tidal wave” of forever chemicals production to meet demand…

blocks.text: Pfas companies are launching a “tidal wave” of forever chemicals production to meet demand from the AI industry, a campaign organisation has warned.
Despite alarm over the chemicals, which have been linked to cancer, a survey of the 10 biggest manufacturers found most had plans to increase production.
Many frame their investments around the “AI revolution”, because of the role Pfas play in semiconductor production and next-generation datacentre cooling systems.

But opponents warn that the chemicals, which never degrade in nature, are a ticking timebomb for human and planetary health. They say increased production risks undermining nascent moves to restrict Pfas in Europe, the UK and parts of the US.

“These companies’ expansion plans show that unless governments and regulators insist on a rapid phaseout, we will face a new tidal wave of forever chemicals,” said Anne-Sofie Bäckar, the executive director of ChemSec, the Swedish chemicals watchdog that carried out the research.
ChemSec’s survey found nearly all of the 10 biggest manufacturers of Pfas had plans to increase production, at sites in Europe, Asia and North America.
The boom in AI tech was leading demand, with Pfas used for “eco-friendly” datacentre cooling and in various stages of semiconductor manufacturing.

Japan-headquarted Daikin said it was launching a “datacentre hub” to meet demand, and promised to “maintain and expand our top share in the industry by expanding sales of existing fluorine products and introducing new products”.

The French multinational Arkema was expanding its refrigerant offering, with a new $60m (£44m) production unit in Kentucky that it said “will enable us to follow the rapid expansion of datacenters’ cooling needs”.

And the US Pfas producer Chemours was expanding to meet demand from “advanced datacenters and AI hardware”. It said its “innovative liquid cooling solutions” lower the energy, water, space, maintenance and investment costs of datacentres.
Critics have said Chemours – recently ordered to pay $450m to settle a lawsuit over Pfas discharges – downplays the chemicals’ toxicity and climate impact.

Other companies increasing production were Japanese multinational AGC, Chinese conglomerate Dongyue, India-based chemicals giant Gujarat Fluorochemicals, secretive Russian Pfas producer HaloPolymer, Mexico’s Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials, US-based fluorinated gases producer Solstice and Belgian multinational Syensqo.

Producers also cited Pfas coatings and binders for lithium-ion batteries, used in EVs, laptops and phones, as a parallel growth area. Gujarat Fluorochemicals’ chief executive, Bir Kapoor, recently identified batteries as one of several “sunrise sectors”, alongside datacentres, semiconductors and green hydrogen. “There is a tremendous growth opportunity there,” he said.
The only clear exceptions were the Swiss company Archroma, which was switching to marketing Pfas-free alternatives, and the German giant BASF, which has said it will exit Pfas production by 2028.
after newsletter promotion

Pfas are used for a new form of datacentre cooling touted as more water- and energy-efficient. In “two-phase immersion cooling” systems, servers are immersed in a pool of Pfas with a low boiling point. As the hardware gets hot, the fluid boils, drawing heat away as vapour. That rises to a water-cooled condensing coil at the top of the tank, cools back to a liquid state and re-enters the cycle.
Pfas also play a crucial role in the fabrication process for semiconductors, another sector booming to meet demand from the AI industry.

According to a recent investor note from Danske Bank: “In the world of microchips, these ‘forever chemicals’ are not merely peripheral additives; they are essential ingredients integrated into as many as 1,000 distinct steps at the nanometric level.”
But analysts also warned Pfas were “the hidden risk of the AI boom” with “escalating potential for multibillion-euro remediation and litigation liabilities”.
The carbon-fluorine bonds in Pfas, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are among the strongest in organic chemistry, rendering them incredibly resistant to heat, water and corrosion.

That makes them useful for a range of industrial processes and consumer products. But it also makes them virtually indestructible in the natural environment. As a result, they continue to be recycled through planetary systems, leading to their accumulation in air, water and soil, and up the food chain.
Although Pfas have existed for less than a century, scientists have warned that their accumulation in the environment has already breached a planetary boundary.
Already the chemicals are thought to contaminate the blood of nearly every living person. Research links them to cancer, liver disease, kidney issues, high cholesterol and birth defects.
ChemSec sent finger-prick blood tests to the chief executives of all the European companies in its top 10, encouraging them to test Pfas levels in their own blood and share the results publicly.
“The people who lead them must understand that they too are affected by the toxins they produce, which have been detected in the blood of more than 99% of people worldwide,” said Bäckar.

articles.title: President, VP barred from businesses due to 'greater possibility of abuse' -- Cabotaje-Tang
articles.summary: Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang on Monday explained that the President and Vice President are barred from participating in any business because of the greater possibility…

blocks.text: Published September 14, 2026 1:49pm

Former Sandiganbayan presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang on Monday explained that the President and Vice President are barred from participating in any business because of the greater possibility of abuse of power in their respective offices, being the country’s two highest government officials.

On the 24th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Senator-Judge Panfilo Lacson asked Cabotaje-Tang why the ban on business participation applies only to the President and Vice President and not to governors, mayors, senators, and members of the House of Representatives.

“Given the fact that the President and Vice President are the two highest officials of the land, ang sinasabi doon [it’s stated that], there is the greater possibility of abuse in their office,” Cabotaje-Tang said.

“They have greater powers, as stated by the Supreme Court. That’s why the prohibitions are more stringent for them, and because of the powers that they wield, there is a greater possibility of abuse in their office,” she added.

Cabotaje-Tang said Republic Act No. 6713, or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, also provides prohibitions for other government officials, but affirmed that the restriction is “absolute” for the President and Vice President, as well as their spouses.

Article VII, Section 13 of the Constitution states that the President, Vice President, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants shall not, during their tenure, directly or indirectly practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise or special privilege granted by the government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or -controlled corporations or their subsidiaries.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero then asked Tang why the Constitution specifically states that the officials mentioned shall not “participate in any business” rather than “have an interest in any business.”
“What does that mean? Does it mean they can’t own a business, or that they can’t participate in a business they own—meaning, actively run it?” Escudero asked.
Tang, in response, said the term “participate” refers to direct or indirect participation.
“Meaning whether ownership in a corporation or participating either as a director or as an officer of the corporation, that is prohibited,” she said.
Escudero then clarified whether it was Tang’s position that a President or Vice President should divest from any business they own, even a sari-sari store, after taking their oath of office.
“Yes, sir. In fact, under the law, there is a need to divest upon assumption of office immediately, and within 30 days,” Tang said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Monday briefing: What do Reform’s record-setting donations mean for the party – and our politics?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: As Labour MPs scramble to realign later today around a bill that could stop donations like this in their tracks, a look at new game-changing donations to a party engulfed in…

blocks.text: Good morning. Nigel Farage has a confirmed talent for upending the laws of political gravity, and this weekend has been no exception, as he declared himself “humbled” by two donations of £36m each from cryptocurrency tycoons Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
I’d shoehorn a joke about buses in here but, honestly, this feels too consequential for that.
The largest single donations in British political history were made after a dismal party conference, the substance of which was all but obscured by the financial scandals engulfing Reform.

As the financial dubiety continues, and the numbers of millions tick upwards to seem almost meaningless, it might be tempting to roll your eyes and focus elsewhere – but this is not the time to look away. These are gamechanging donations, transformative if used effectively at this stage in the election cycle, just as Labour has regained its confidence and the Tories are contemplating a comeback.

As a bill that could stop donations like this in their tracks returns to the Lords later today, I spoke to Jessica Elgot, the Guardian’s deputy political editor, about what these millions mean and why they matter. First, a wrap-up of this weekend’s headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: Economy | Former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit – and that rejoining the European Union’s customs union would be the fastest route to recovery.

Technology | Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace” of AI development. Amodei had cautioned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year.

Sweden | With most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority.

Ukraine | A train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways.

Travel | The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.

blocks.text: In depth: More money, more problems?

blocks.caption: ‘Competitive spirit’ … Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo. Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/Ben Delo Foundation

blocks.text: Let’s start with more detail on the donations, by businessmen who have amassed astronomical fortunes trading in cryptocurrency. Ben Delo, a previous Reform donor, has given £36m. Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned by Donald Trump last year.

(A brief note here on how that story came to light: the Sunday Times approached Reform and Farage after a confidential source told them that Delo had donated to the party. Soon after, the Telegraph published an opinion piece by Delo himself, announcing the donation and trouncing the Sunday Times scoop. As Sunday Times political editor Ben Riley-Smith noted on X: “A fundamental part of political reporting – approaching for comment before publishing – just totally breaks down if this is what happens. Bad for both sides: Will increase the chance of inaccuracies.” Reform has used the same tactic with the Guardian, as we talked about in a previous newsletter.)

Less than 24 hours later, another crypto donor was troubling the Telegraph’s op-ed page: this time Christopher Harborne – whose previous £5m gift to Farage is the one currently subject to a parliamentary standards investigation – announcing he had likewise donated £36m, saying: “My competitive spirit inspired me to match [Delo].”

Taken together, these donations are unprecedented in British political history: £72m is bigger than the total sum spent by the seven largest parties in the last general election (about £67.9m) and almost double the total donations to all political parties so far this year (about £41.8m).
Are these donations legal?

“There’s nothing wrong with these donations that we know of,” says Jessica, her final four words doing a lot of heavy lifting in present circumstances. The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into that £5m Harborne gift, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024 and first revealed by the Guardian. Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.

It’s a legal requirement for every party to rigorously check the sources of donations, and, doing the media rounds yesterday, Reform’s economics spokesperson Robert Jenrick was sounding supremely confident that the donations were “entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, what it is going to be in the future”.

Jenrick was referencing the representation of the people bill, going through parliament, which will bring in more stringent rules about foreign donations. Gifts to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March. Delo has recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong, while Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand.

I don’t have space to get into it here, but if you’re curious about the path to becoming a crypto billionaire and the people who get trampled along the way, I’d recommend the actor and crypto investigator Ben McKenzie’s excellent film Everybody Is Lying to You for Money. (Yes, he’s Ryan in The OC).
How could Reform spend the money?

Reform has already vastly scaled up its party infrastructure since the general election, moving to new offices in London’s Millbank Tower, once synonymous with New Labour election operations. Press officers, graphic designers, videographers and regional organisers have augmented staffing capacity, but their wider policy offering is still weak. An injection of cash will probably mean more hires to address this, and perhaps even drafting legislation to boost Farage’s projection of a party that’s ready for government.
Reform is expected to install campaign managers and branch coordinators in hundreds of seats across the country – as their list of 60-plus job vacancies indicates.

And if this newsletter gig doesn’t work out for me, I might throw my bunnet in for the senior writer role advertised here – the application requires a 500-word letter, written in the style of Zia Yusuf, “setting out how the political class broke Britain and how Reform UK will fix it”.

The donations also promise a massive boost to Reform’s visibility – they can pay for the big “air war” expenses incurred in coming byelections and council elections next year, more locally targeted online advertising and billboards, as well as getting creative with its TV studios.
Reform now has the money to focus on labour-intensive data gathering in target constituencies as well, says Jessica, who predicts it will be “transformative” for the party.

“You’ve got enough money now to spend on the granular and expensive work of going around every single constituency in the country making sure your data about voters, and non-voters, is bang on. And if you’re a party that wants to show that you’re on the march, they’ve got the momentum, you can dominate the airwaves, dominate people’s social media feeds.”
Will this prompt a rethink on a cap for all donations?

Labour MPs’ WhatsApp chats have been popping off over the weekend, Jessica reports, with anger that the government did not act last week to restrict domestic donations in the elections bill. Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, pulled her amendment proposing an annual cap of £100,000 after Andy Burnham dropped his support for it, following intensive lobbying from the party’s trade union backers, who argued it would undermine their ability to donate to the party.

But the bill has its second reading in the Lords later today and, yesterday, communities secretary Angela Rayner suggested that the government was still considering amendments and that “it’s not as simple as we’re saying we won’t put a cap”.

As Sunday turned into Monday, some unions appeared to be shifting their opposition while Labour MPs and donors were urging the government to look again at party funding rules. But Reform argues that – as a relatively new political force – it needs this cash injection to level the playing field with other parties and their far longer-standing donor arrangements.
What about an early election?

As Jessica reminds me, Reform will be able to splash its cash in the coming months because many restrictions on party spending don’t kick in until a general election is called. “Other parties are not spending that money now because they don’t have it. And their donors are not giving money at this stage in the cycle. So they won’t have any competition for those eyeballs whatsoever.”

There’s growing chatter in Westminster that – if economic growth continues to inch upwards and Reform remains static in the polls – Burnham may go for an early summer general election next year. (With a note of caution from Jessica that there will probably be a backlash from hundreds of Labour MPs on course to lose their seats.)

A major consideration for the prime minister is, of course, Reform – which remains, in recent polls, a couple of points behind Labour and a similar amount ahead of the Tories. According to Jenrick on Sunday, these donations enable his party to be “battle ready”, whatever Burnham decides. Meanwhile, Labour sent out an “urgent” fundraising appeal over the weekend, warning that Reform could “simply drown Labour’s message out in elections to come”.

Clearly, £72m in cash is good for Reform. “But whether it re-energises the party, and voters think, ‘People are willing to give this money millions of pounds because they offer a radical reset and I want that, too’ or whether it adds to that perception of a party being bought by billionaires, it’s hard to say.”
after newsletter promotion

Crucially, it keeps everybody talking about Reform’s finances. After a summer marred by scandal, internal divisions and a damp squib byelection, and at a point when Farage’s own popularity ratings have plummeted and support for the party has stalled, that is last place Reform wants to be.
The week to come

items: Monday | First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff to discuss moves towards self-determination across the nations.

Tuesday | The final report of the Thirwall Inquiry into events at the neonatal unit where Lucy Letby worked will be published. Letby was sentenced to 15 whole-life terms for murdering seven infants and attempting to murder seven others.
Thursday | Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, will address the European parliament.

blocks.text: What else we’ve been enjoying

blocks.caption: Our democracy won’t survive the death of reading, writes John Harris. Illustration: Ben Jennings/The Guardian

items: Much of the hand-wringing around the death of reading can seem uncircumstantial, but not this excellent column from John Harris on what it could mean for the future of our democracy in a time of “nonsense and poison”. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team

Anyone who, like me, has returned to the place they grew up to see if mere proximity can transport them, in spirit, back to their youth will inhale this thoughtful and emotive collection of mini-essays by Deborah Levy, Julia Samuels and other novelists on revisiting their childhood homes. Here be ghosts. Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team

Our This is how we do it series is a must-read, and this piece from a couple on making time for sex alongside their open relationship and raising three young kids is no exception (not least to understand how they possibly find the time). Charlie

blocks.text: Sport

blocks.caption: Alexander Zverev celebrates with the US Open trophy after beating Ben Shelton. Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

blocks.text: Tennis | Alexander Zverev, the No 1 seed, beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2, the American’s hopes dashed in his first grand slam final.
Golf | The captain Anna Nordqvist led Europe to a 15-13 victory in the Solheim Cup a month after retiring from competitive golf.

Football | Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea dominated in a 5-0 away victory against Eva Olid’s Manchester United, while Pro Ref admitted Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s Manchester derby should not have counted after the VAR ruled Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup.
The front pages

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “Revealed: true scale of Britain’s involvement in the slave trade”, is the Guardian’s splash today.

The Telegraph leads with “Hospitality chiefs urge PM to cut VAT” and the Express says “Labour tourist tax will hammer seaside B&Bs”. The i Paper’s headline is “Reform’s £72m crypto bonanza sparks Labour donations row”, Metro says “Labour threat to Reform’s £72m windfall”, while the Mirror’s take is “Bitcon?”. The FT’s splash is “Trump rejects industry calls for brake on AI over fears of losing race to China”.
The Sun has “Boris flees Vlad drone blitz”, the Mail asks “Did Putin drone target Boris and top security officials?”
Today in Focus

blocks.caption: Warnings over AI are not new. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters

blocks.text: AI isn’t going to end humanity … right?

Ten per cent. That’s the risk, more or less, claimed a high-profile AI developer last week, that the technology wipes humanity out in the next decade. “I think it’s a crossover moment for the AI safety story because this has been for a long time talked about inside the AI world”, says our UK technology editor, Robert Booth, “but now, the general public and the political class have become increasingly concerned about it.” So how worried, asks Annie Kelly, should we be?
Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld

blocks.caption: Illustration: Tom Gauld/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: ‘People seem really happy it’s open again.’ The Au Bon Accueil restaurant in Saint-Martin-sur-Ouanne.  Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian

blocks.text: “In bistros and cafes, people don’t just eat and drink, they catch up with each other, meet new people, debate, laugh, read, write and sometimes fall in love,” said Alain Fontaine of Paris’s Le Mesturet bistro. Yet where once there were an estimated 500,000 cafe-bistros dotted throughout France, there are now only about 30,000 to 40,000. But one group of local campaigners in the northern Burgundy community of Saint-Martin-sur-Ouanne has saved one such establishment, and in the process, make their village livable again.

After a successful community-led campaign to reopen it, Au Bon Acceuil cafe-bistro has been brought back to life – and every table is taken. As the village mayor, Hervé Chapuis, put it: “Our aim is to keep this kind of business open to support the social fabric. It’s part of village life and people missed it. Now, village life has returned to its proper rhythm.”

articles.title: 'Safeguard the ballot': Marcos appeals to voters as BARMM goes to polls
articles.summary: His appeal came as violence and ballot issues disrupted voting in several areas.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 1:35pm
This photo shows President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. giving message to BARMM voters in a video statement released on September 14, 2026.
Screengrab / PCO

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. encouraged voters to protect the integrity of their votes and preserve peace during the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
In a video statement released Monday, September 14, Marcos called the BARMM elections a "milestone" in the region's transition toward democratic governance and self-determination.
"I therefore encourage every qualified voter to take part in this momentous event with wisdom, dignity, and respect for one another," Marcos said.

Data from the Commission on Elections (Comelec) show there are 2,393,202 registered voters in BARMM expected to participate in the elections. Comelec Chairman George Garcia said in August that the poll body was hoping for a 75% voter turnout.
The polls are intended to establish a democratically elected Bangsamoro government and fill the 80-seat parliament.
"Let us also safeguard the integrity of the ballot and preserve the peace that has made this democratic exercise possible," Marcos said.
'Safety, transparency'

Election watchdog Legal Network for Truthful Elections (LENTE) Philippines, meanwhile, called for immediate de-escalation and transparency following reports of gunfire and alleged ballot mishandling in several areas.
This came after Comelec placed Cotabato City and Maluso, Basilan, under its control following incidents of violence and the discovery of pre-shaded ballots.
At least three people were killed and 15 others wounded in a shooting in Cotabato City involving supporters of rival political parties.
In Maluso, Comelec found that ballots in 36 of the municipality's 68 precincts had been compromised and pre-shaded.

"The bombings and gunfire in Cotabato City and the reported ballot-handling violations in Lanao del Sur and Tawi-Tawi in the opening hours of voting underscore the need for immediate corrective and protective action. LENTE calls on all stakeholders to proceed towards the path of de-escalation as tension continues to rise throughout the start of the electoral process," LENTE said in a statement.

articles.title: Hyrox athlete sparks debate for continuing race after soiling herself
articles.summary: Some have raised concerns around hygiene while others saluted her resolve to finish the race.

blocks.text: An athlete's Hyrox performance has sparked debate after completing a race in Beijing despite soiling herself midway through the event.

Footage of the woman competing in the indoor fitness competition despite her soiled legs has gone viral, with some people raising concerns around hygiene and others saluting her resolve to push through. Some also criticised race organisers for letting her to continue.
Hyrox said they launched a "major cleanup operation" after the event on Saturday, including by sanitising equipment and replacing sections of the carpet.
The German fitness company acknowledged the "legitimate concerns" but urged people not to direct their frustration at the athlete herself.
The company did not reveal the woman's identity, but it was revealed online and she subsequently received threats of violence.
"There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete," Hyrox said in a statement early on Monday.
"Any person identified as engaging in this behaviour – whether through comments, direct messages or social media – will be permanently banned from all Hyrox events," it said.
Some participants in the same event had demanded an apology and a refund, arguing that they were forced to come into contact with contaminated equipment, Chinese media reported.
In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, such as the sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world.
Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including spitting and littering.

"From a basic health and sanitation standpoint, the athlete should have been stopped immediately, and any contaminated areas should have been closed off and properly cleaned before other athletes were allowed through," Erica Dodge, a US-based nurse, wrote in a comment on Instagram.

Joe Ho, who also took part in the Hyrox Beijing competition over the weekend, has criticised Hyrox's response to the issue and called on the organisation to "take responsibility when its own procedures fail".
"If the organisation accepts that something went wrong, why not offer affected participants refunds, credits, or some meaningful form of compensation?" he wrote.
Others in the fitness community have pointed out that this is not unheard of for endurance athletes.
One comment on Facebook, whose author noted that marathoners have similar experiences, while another wrote: "They've trained too long and too hard to give up just like that."

In 2005, British marathoner Paula Radcliffe famously stopped at the 22-mile mark during the London Marathon to relieve herself by the side of the road in full view of cameras and then went on to win the race.
Earlier this year, Chinese marathoner Li Meizhen made headlines after crossing the finish line at the Hengshui Lake Marathon with menstrual blood on her legs.

articles.title: Romualdez’s transfer to Payatas ordered after PGH assessment
articles.summary: (Updated) The order came after UP-PGH found him clinically stable and determined that continued hospital confinement was not medically necessary.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 1:32pm

Rep. Martin Romualdez (Leyte) lies in a hospital bed at Cardinal Santos Medical Center as police place him under custody on Sept. 7, 2026, following the Sandiganbayan's issuance of a warrant in a P7.44-billion plunder case.
Philstar.com / Contributed photo

MANILA, Philippines (Updated 1:48 p.m.) — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered the transfer of former House speaker and incumbent Rep. Martin Romualdez (Leyte) to the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory in Barangay Payatas on Monday, September 14.

The anti-graft court issued the order following findings by University of the Philippines-Philippine General Hospital (UP-PGH) officials that he was "clinically stable" and there was "no imperative medical need" for his continued hospital confinement.
Romualdez is to be held at the Quezon City jail as a "detention prisoner," the anti-graft court said.
UP-PGH Director Dr. Gerardo Legaspi said Romualdez's risk of an impending heart attack was low, while his hypertension, diabetes and chronic cerebrovascular disease were controlled.
Romualdez had been confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City when the anti-graft court ordered his arrest over a plunder case.
On September 12, he was transferred to UP-PGH for an independent medical assessment to determine whether continued hospital confinement was necessary.

The court ordered the arrest of Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co and two others after the Office of the Ombudsman charged them with plunder over alleged kickbacks worth P7.44 billion from flood-control, infrastructure and other government projects.
In a statement, Romualdez maintained his innocence and said he would face the charges and address the allegations before the proper court.

"I thank my physicians at Cardinal Santos Medical Center and the doctors of the Philippine General Hospital for their care and professional judgment. I will continue to follow the medical advice of my doctors," Romualdez said.
"I have always said that I will face the charges against me and answer them before the proper court. That has not changed," he added.
Romualdez will be the third incumbent lawmaker detained at the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory.
Sens. Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada are also detained at the Payatas facility over separate plunder cases.

articles.title: Cuban dance teacher ordered EU sabotage attacks from Russia
articles.summary: In 2024, a Cuban man coordinated a series of arson attacks in four EU countries while operating on behalf of Russian intelligence services. DW Investigations tracked him back to a Latin dance studio…
articles.byline: Mathias Bölinger, Julett Pineda, Anna Chaika

image.caption: Oemis Romagoza Durruthy teaches Latin dance in northern RussiaImage: vk.ru

blocks.text: On social media platforms, the man called himself "Adrian" or "Dios," meaning "God” in Spanish. In 2024, accounts linked to the man posted job ads on Telegram. "Work as a photographer," one offered in Russian in a chat about opportunities in Poland. "To those interested in applying, send resume, phone number and passport," another advertised in a group for Cuban expatriates in Russia. "Looking for people with military experience in monitoring, intelligence, logistics and tactical maneuvers," one said in Spanish in a group for Latinos, promising $1,500 plus a bonus for each operation completed.

Dios lured multiple people into carrying out sabotage for Russia in at least four EU countries, an investigation by DW and three other European broadcasters has found. Most of the recruits came from Spanish-speaking countries.

For months, DW and its partners conducted dozens of interviews with security officials and people close to the suspects. We pieced together classified court documents, official statements, social media posts and leaked data to find out who Dios is and reconstruct how he built a network of saboteurs to commit arson attacks across Europe.
Not all of them completed their tasks.
Recruiting vulnerable people
One of the people Dios recruited was Luis Alfonso Murillo Diosa, who was 34 years old at the time.

Originally from Caicedo, a rural town in western Colombia known for its mountainous landscapes and its crops, Murillo was raised in a family of coffee farmers. But several years of poor harvests pushed the business into debt, according to someone close to the family.

Murillo spent six years in the Colombian army. According to court documents, he left in 2015. He then hopped between jobs like many ex-soldiers, juggling barista courses, stints as a bodyguard and his family's coffee business.
In early 2024, Murillo decided to enlist in the Ukrainian army, where foreign fighters can earn a few thousand euros a month when deployed to the front line, court documents show.
Looking for information about the process, he joined a Facebook group for Latin Americans seeking to fight in Ukraine. That's when he was contacted by Dios.

"It's often vulnerable people who are being targeted,” said Daniela Richterova, an associate professor in Intelligence Studies at King's College London. "Vulnerable people who need money and are willing to travel for money and are willing to not ask many questions about the purpose of what they're carrying out."

blocks.caption: Murillo said he sought to join the Ukrainian army, not work for RussiaImage: Facebook

blocks.text: Arrested for attempted sabotage

In a private Facebook message, Dios introduced himself as a member of a "special group," and asked Murillo to work with him on "special missions" in Europe instead of going to Ukraine, according to classified court documents reviewed by DW.
Murillo took the offer, and Dios organized everything remotely: flight tickets, accommodation, ground transport. They never met in person.

Once Murillo reached Bucharest in July 2024, Dios sent him a satellite image with a recycling facility and an oil well marked. Murillo was supposed to take photos and videos of the locations — and later start a fire. However, he was detained while walking near the recycling facility one night after taking photos. According to court records, Murillo told investigators that he never intended to commit arson. He said he was trying to get to Europe to reach Ukraine, and didn't know for whom he was working.
In 2025, Murillo was sentenced to six years in prison for attempted sabotage.
Russia's 'disposable agents'

DW and its partners have confirmed that Murillo was one of at least a dozen people recruited by Dios for acts of sabotage across Europe. Such recruits are frequently referred to as "disposable agents": people often hired online who at times don't even know the identities of their employers or the real aim of their assignments.

The Kremlin has increasingly used disposable agents after EU governments expelled scores of Russian diplomats suspected of espionage and disinformation following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the conflict researcher Keir Giles told DW.

"That left a gap in Russia's capability, and it took time for them to find this new means of recruiting random people to carry out sometimes apparently random attacks," said Giles, who has written several books about Russia's military.

In 2024 alone, disposable agents burned down a shopping center in Poland, set fire to an Ikea store in Lithuania and delivered incendiary packages that ignited at logistics hubs in several countries. German authorities said throwaway agents, as they are also called, steered a drone with explosives toward a Ukrainian freight plane in Leipzig in August.

blocks.caption: The 2024 attack on a Warsaw shopping center has been attributed to disposable agentsImage: Attila Husejnow/SOPA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The suspected perpetrators of such attacks are often not Russian — nor do they have a known prior connection to Russian intelligence services. Many of the people prosecuted have been Ukrainian refugees, low-level criminals or local youths looking to make quick money.

"Russia doesn't have to be particularly careful about covering its tracks, because there is no downside to being detected," Giles said. "And, of course, it boosts the idea that Russia wants to project that it is omnipotent, that it can cause damage wherever."
Russian arson made in Cuba

DW confirmed that, over a span of four months in 2024, Dios instructed his recruits to set fire to two construction-supply businesses in Poland, a bus garage in the Czech Republic, a recycling facility in Romania and equipment destined for Ukraine produced by a company in Lithuania.

Lithuanian prosecutors were the only ones to publicly attribute the series of arson attacks to Russia's military intelligence service, known as GRU. They also put a Cuban man living in Russia on an international wanted list.
After reviewing classified court documents and dozens of leaked files, DW and its partners were able to confirm that Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy is the man behind the alias Dios.

blocks.caption: Lithuanian prosecution has added Oemis Romagoza Durruthy to an international wanted listImage: LRT

blocks.text: Born in Camaguey, Cuba's third-largest city, Romagoza has lived in Russia for at least seven years.

A Latin dance teacher in the northern Russian city of Petrozavodsk, Romagoza is listed as a contact person on the social media channels of a local dance studio, Made in Cuba. In dozens of online videos of his dance classes, he shows off his salsa, bachata and kizomba steps.

Romagoza married a Russian woman in 2022 and later obtained Russian citizenship. A series of wedding to photos DW found on social media show the couple posing next to a grand piano. Other pictures show them with their two children.

DW was unable to determine when and how he came to work on behalf of Russia's secret services. Leaked data indicate that Romagoza might have run into financial trouble. In 2023, he borrowed money from several credit lenders. In one of the entries, he listed a supermarket chain as his employer.

A few months later, Romagoza joined several Facebook groups of Latin Americans looking for work in Poland or seeking to fight for Ukraine. Around the same time, Dios started posting job offers on Telegram.

blocks.caption: Born in Cuba, Romagoza has lived in Russia for at least seven yearsImage: Instagram

blocks.text: Sabotage continues in EU
It is unclear whether Dios continued recruiting people or directed more attacks after September 2024. But Russia's relentless sabotage campaign across Europe hasn't stopped.

In August alone, Estonia arrested two suspects for an arson attack targeting a company that supplies unmanned military vehicles to Ukraine, and Poland reported fires at two other facilities where components for drones and helicopters are manufactured. Authorities in both countries suspect that Russia is behind the plots.

"It seems like there are still people out there who are either naive enough or are really hungry for money and motivated by monetary rewards for these kinds of activities," said Richterova, whose research focuses on Russian intelligence.
At least nine of the disposable agents Romagoza recruited have been caught. Two are serving sentences of six to eight years for attempted sabotage or terrorism. Others are currently awaiting trial.

Meanwhile, European authorities are still after Romagoza, who might still be in Russia. In April, the Made in Cuba studio posted a video of him teaching a salsa class. Romagoza is seen facing the mirror, leading a group of women who follow his steps and his commands. "Because that is what I am. In heaven, I am the chief," sings the Cuban salsa tune playing in the background.
Around the same time the Latin dance studio posted the video, Romagoza joined at least two more Facebook groups for Latin Americans looking for work in Poland.
Oemis Romagoza Durruthy did not reply to requests for comment.

articles.title: Unexplained wealth can be ground for public official's removal -- Cabotaje-Tang
articles.summary: A public official"s acquisition of unexplained wealth can be a ground for removal from office, former Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang said Monday.

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 14, 2026 1:08pm
A public official’s acquisition of unexplained wealth can be a ground for removal from office, former Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang said Monday.

Tang gave the testimony during Day 24 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, where she was presented as an expert on public accountability and anti-corruption laws, including the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, Civil Forfeiture Law, and the law governing Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs).

House prosecutor and Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno said the prosecution presented Tang as a witness to provide the senator-judges and the public with a legal framework on how the anti-graft court assesses evidence involving properties acquired by public officials while in office.

Following an objection from the defense panel, the impeachment court presiding officer, Sen. Francis Escudero, ruled that Tang was not testifying on the specific allegations raised by the prosecution in the impeachment case against Duterte.
During her direct examination, Tang said a public official found to have unexplained wealth could result in his or her removal or dismissal under existing anti-corruption laws.
“What it means is that if a public officer is found to have unexplained wealth in accordance with Republic Act 1379, that is a ground for removal or dismissal under Republic Act 3019,” she said.

Republic Act No. 1379, or the law declaring the forfeiture in favor of the State of property found to have been unlawfully acquired by a public officer or employee, provides for the forfeiture of such property.
Republic Act No. 3019, meanwhile, is the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.

Tang likewise confirmed that a public official’s property is presumed to have been unlawfully acquired if it is proven that the property was acquired during the official’s incumbency at a cost “manifestly out of proportion to his/her salary as public officer or employee and to his/her other lawful income and the income from legitimately acquired property” under RA 1379.
Tang, however, clarified that the presumption that a property was unlawfully acquired does not amount to a guilty verdict for a crime.

“If it is shown that an official acquired property that is grossly or manifestly disproportionate to his salary, lawful income and income from lawfully acquired properties, it is presumed to have been unlawfully acquired. This presumption, however, is rebuttable,” Tang said.
“This means that if a public official can satisfactorily explain how he or she lawfully acquired those properties, that presumption will no longer apply,” she added.
Tang was presented as a prosecution witness under Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which alleges that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth through the following:

items: failure to fully and truthfully disclose all her and her spouse’s assets, liabilities and net worth in their Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), including her SALNs for 2022, 2023 and 2024; and
failure to divest, and instead willfully continuing, all her business interests during her tenure as vice president in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

blocks.text: During a House justice committee hearing on the impeachment complaints against Duterte in April, lawyer Karen Batu, the SALN custodian of the Office of the Ombudsman, confirmed that the vice president did not declare any cash on hand or bank deposits in her SALNs from 2019 to 2024.
Duterte has no declared cash on hand, bank deposits from 2019 to 2024, the SALNs reportedly showed.
“Based on the submitted SALNs, walang nakalagay na cash on hand or deposit (Based on the submitted SALNs, there was none),” Batu then told the House committee.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Sydney mayor allegedly threatened and children secretly recorded after he refused to step down, Icac hears
articles.summary: Corruption inquiry turns its investigation to allegations Strathfield councillors may have engaged in blackmail or illegal surveillance

blocks.text: A Sydney mayor was allegedly threatened, followed and his children were secretly recorded after he refused to honour an agreement to step down, the NSW corruption watchdog has heard.
Former independent Strathfield council mayor Matthew Blackmore has fronted the New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) inquiry, codenamed Operation Rosny.

The inquiry is investigating accusations levelled against former Labor councillors Sharangan Maheswaran and Karen Pensabene, including whether they engaged in blackmail or possible surveillance against Blackmore.

Blackmore in 2022 had initially agreed to split the mayoralty, so he would take the position first before resigning to allow a Labor councillor, which was expected to be Pensabene, to finish the term, he told the commission.
Maheswaran wanted to ensure Labor leadership at the council, state and federal level before the 2023 state election to bolster campaign efforts, Icac heard.
But in January 2023, Blackmore revealed to the two Labor councillors he wanted to stay on as mayor, which led them to become agitated and upset, he said.

Maheswaran allegedly told Blackmore: “What you’ve got to understand, Matthew … I’ve got a reputation in the party that if I don’t like someone, they don’t get away with crossing me. It would take me about six weeks to take you down.”
Blackmore responded by saying he could “get fucked”.
Blackmore told the commission his wife had taken a photo of Maheswaran’s car on the street outside their home, which was near a brothel.
Asked if he was aware this photo could be used to his political advantage, he said he only wanted it to check if the number plate was Maheswaran’s.
Blackmore had seen the car in front of his house a number of times and was “a bit intimidated as to whether he was stalking my house,” he told the commission.
Pensabene later messaged Blackmore to warn him Maheswaran was “out of control”, and said he was printing 20,000 attack flyers.
One of the flyers, which Blackmore referred to as a “shit sheet”, was left on the former mayor’s car, and Pensabene warned him that “everything so far is less than 10% of what is coming”.
At a later meeting, Maheswaran told Blackmore he’d had operatives following him for five months, taking photos and recording his conversations without his knowledge, according to Blackmore.
Blackmore took it to mean they were going to continue releasing media stories if he didn’t resign as mayor.
after newsletter promotion
Soon after, he began receiving inquiries from journalists working for News Corp and YouTuber FriendlyJordies.

According to a statement from Blackmore, Maheswaran told him: “All of this will go away when you resign from the mayoralty. It will stop. You’re not going to have any harassment as long as you agree with us to do this.”
Maheswaran also alleged Blackmore had used the mayoralty vehicle to take a family holiday and told him the location of the vacation.
“The holiday thing was one of the worst because we weren’t actually intending to go and our plans were changed last minute so no one really knew where I was going,” Blackmore said.
The entire situation has changed his sense of personal safety.
“I can’t go to sleep without checking my house is locked,” Blackmore said.
In a text to Pensabene, he wrote: “I feel sick that my children have been surveillanced [sic] by Sharangan’s undercover people.”
Maheswaran is due to appear at Icac on Friday.

articles.title: Historic BARMM vote opens under shadow of killings, ballot tampering
articles.summary: Comelec has taken control of Cotabato, Maluso as BARMM voting opens.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 11:59am

MANILA, Philippines — Voters across the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao began casting ballots Monday, September 14, in the region's first parliamentary elections, as violence and reports of election irregularities disrupted voting in several areas.
At least three people were killed and 15 others wounded in Cotabato City hours before polls opened, while authorities also reported gunfire, an explosion and alleged pre-shaded ballots in Basilan.

The Commission on Elections later placed Cotabato City and Maluso, Basilan under Comelec control, giving the poll body direct authority over local officials, government employees and law enforcement to address security threats and protect the integrity of the vote.
More than two million voters are eligible to elect 80 members of the first regular Bangsamoro Parliament, marking a major step in a peace process that established BARMM after decades of conflict.
In Marawi City, voters formed long lines outside polling stations early Monday as soldiers, police personnel and armored vehicles stood guard, Agence France-Presse reported.
"We're excited, we came here early in the morning," 18-year-old voter Mohammad Actar Macabada told AFP after casting his ballot.
"I'm nervous because there might be chaos. Before there was chaos. Now it's peaceful," he said. "I'm excited for the results."
More than 20,000 security personnel have been deployed across BARMM, with quick response teams placed on standby.
Explosion near polling area
An explosion, meanwhile, also reported Sunday evening in MB Kalanganan, Cotabato City.
Police said a male resident of Poblacion 1 was injured after he saw a bright light and heard a blast while waiting for his construction foreman.
Comelec Chairman George Garcia said the Philippine National Police later determined that the blast involved an improvised explosive device.
AFP separately reported that a man died in hospital early Monday following an explosion near another polling station. Police were still investigating its cause.
The incidents were among those cited by Comelec in placing Cotabato City under its control.
"Just earlier, the Commission en banc decided to place Cotabato City under Comelec control," Garcia said.

Placing an area under Comelec control gives the poll body direct supervision over government officials and law enforcement involved in the election. The declaration also allows it to direct security deployments and other measures needed to protect the vote.
Pre-shaded ballots in Basilan
Comelec also placed Maluso, Basilan under its control after authorities discovered that ballots in 36 of the municipality's 68 precincts had allegedly been pre-shaded overnight.
"We determined as of last night that the ballots in 36 of the 68 precincts had been compromised. We found that all of them had been pre-shaded," Garcia said in mixed English and Filipino.
(Left) Election officers prepare the vote counting machines in a classroom in a voting precinct. (Right) A pre-shaded ballot discovered by the Comelec in Maluso, Basilan.
Commission on Elections / Released
Garcia said election officials had identified those believed responsible and ordered the reprinting of ballots for the affected precincts.
Several ballot boxes also had broken seals, although Garcia said a closer inspection found that the ballots inside other boxes remained intact.
Voting continued as scheduled in Maluso's remaining 32 precincts.

The PPCRV separately reported "rampant" vote buying in Barangays Marang and Gadung in Barira, Maguindanao del Norte, as well as reports of voters casting ballots multiple times at Central Oring Elementary School in Buldon.

As of Monday morning, all clustered precincts in Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Tawi-Tawi and the Special Geographic Area had opened, while 81.46% of clustered precincts in Basilan were operational.
The Bangsamoro polls are the culmination of a decades-long peace process that led to the creation of BARMM and the transition from an appointed interim government to an elected parliament.
Deadly Cotabato shooting

Violence also marked the hours in the leadup the Monday's vote. Before midnight on Sunday, gunfire broke out outside Datu Usman Mampen Elementary School in Cotabato City after supporters of rival political groups jostled for position in a queue ahead of voting.
Cotabato police chief Jibin Bongcayao told AFP that the confrontation began as a struggle over who would vote first.
"It started as a struggle for position in the queue between two groups," Bongcayao said.
"It led to shoving, escalated into a fistfight, and eventually gunfire broke out in a crowded area."
Police confirmed that three men were killed, including an 88-year-old resident, while 15 others were wounded and taken to hospitals.
Scene-of-the-crime operatives recovered shell casings believed to have come from .45-caliber and 9mm firearms.
Bongcayao said those involved belonged to rival political parties that emerged from the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Separate gunfire was also reported Monday at Dilausan Elementary School in Lumbaca-Unayan, Lanao del Sur, according to the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting.
Media reports also cited gunfire at Central Pilot School in Cotabato City, prompting the deployment of Philippine Marines and police. — with Agence France-Presse

articles.title: LPG group asks gov't to suspend excise tax on fuel products
articles.summary: With fuel nearing P100, an oil company and transport groups press government to suspend taxes.

blocks.text: September 14, 2026 | 11:35am
A store helper selling Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) changes the LPG prices on their price board in Paco, Manila on March 25, 2026.
STAR / Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — LPG company REGASCO urged the government to temporarily suspend excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and other fuel products as Dubai crude oil prices remained elevated.

REGASCO and LPG Marketers Association President Arnel Ty said Dubai crude prices are currently above $100 per barrel, prompting the group to write Energy Secretary Sharon Garin to appeal for the suspension of excise taxes.

"Sabi namin, kami po'y umaapela na pupuwede na po siyang magrekomenda sa Department of Finance na suspendihin na po hindi lang [ang excise tax] sa LPG at kerosene, kasama na po ang diesel, gasoline," Ty told dzMM in an interview Monday, September 14.
(We are appealing for her to recommend the suspension of excise taxes not only on LPG and kerosene, but also on diesel and gasoline.)
Ty said if their request for an excise tax suspension is granted, LPG prices may go down by P3 per kilogram, diesel by P6 per liter, gasoline by P10 per liter and kerosene by P5 per liter.
Another round of oil price hikes is expected to take effect Tuesday, September 15, as global oil prices continue to rise due to conflicts affecting the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz.
The latest projected increases could push some fuel products beyond P100 per liter at certain stations.

Under Section 148 of the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended by Republic Act 12316, the president may suspend or reduce excise taxes on petroleum products upon the recommendation of the Development Budget Coordination Committee, in coordination with the Department of Energy, when the one-month average Dubai crude oil price reaches or exceeds $80 per barrel.
Dubai crude is one of the major oil benchmarks used in Asia and influences local fuel pricing.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. exercised the authority earlier this year when he issued Executive Order No. 114 in April, suspending excise taxes on LPG and kerosene for up to three months.
As local fuel prices are expected to rise further this week, transport group MANIBELA launched a two-day transport strike from Monday until Tuesday, September 15.
MANIBELA criticized Secretary Garin's earlier remarks that the government has limited control over local fuel prices because the Philippines imports most of its oil supply.
"For transport workers, however, saying that there is little the government can do is not enough while fuel prices continue to rise and directly eat into their daily income," MANIBELA said.

China has not officially confirmed that the meeting will take place.
Trump on Sunday reiterated his belief that he has a good relationship with Xi.
"I ⁠think ​he's behaved reasonably well, and we ​behave reasonably well," the US president said.
Trump's remarks follow a pattern set by his administration, which has sought to downplay tensions with China, despite frustration in Washington over Beijing's support for Iran.
Trump has previously warned China not to provide Iran with weapons. The US sanctioned three Chinese satellite companies in May for working with Iranian military entities.
China is one of Iran's top economic and diplomatic partners and main buyers of its oil.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA
articles.summary: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’

blocks.text: Israel’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of NAZA, a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.

In the film, the Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza that have killed tens of thousands of civilians. In one interview, a source claims that approval had been given to kill 500 NAZA in order to kill one Hamas member.
The 80-minute documentary won a special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record.
On Sunday Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors on X of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.
“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.
Other Israeli ministers also took aim at the directors, who won an Oscar in 2025 for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
“You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said on X.
“I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms.”

The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, although it is rarely applied. In 2022 the supreme court confirmed that the state may strip people of their nationality if they have failed to show “loyalty”, for example by committing acts of espionage or treason.
The law was also expanded in 2023 to apply to people convicted of “terrorism”.
The law requires the interior minister to submit the revocation request, the justice minister to approve it and judges to validate it.
Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob after the world premiere of 2024’s No Other Land, which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank.

“We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic,” he told the Guardian, adding: “For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons.
“Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”

The Israeli military has responded to NAZA by saying it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary and criticised the use of anonymous testimonies, saying the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified”.

The Palestinian militant group Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Hamas militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza.
The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the subsequent three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties.
– Agence France-Presse contributed to this report
