articles.title: US congressman swims to safety after his plane is forced to land on a lake
articles.summary: The small plane carrying Rep Tom Tiffany had a mechanical issue that forced the pilot to make an emergency landing on a Wisconsin lake.

blocks.text: Wisconsin Congressman Tom Tiffany has said he sustained minor injuries after a plane he was on landed on a lake, forcing him and the pilot to swim to safety.

Tiffany, the state's Republican nominee for governor, was travelling in a small plane on Saturday night when the aircraft encountered a mechanical issue, forcing the pilot to make an emergency landing in Lake Wausau, the county sheriff's office said.
Tiffany said he and the pilot called 911 once they landed.

"As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," Tiffany wrote on social media. The pilot also sustained minor injuries.
Tiffany was coming home from a dinner in La Crosse County when the plane suddenly lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport, he said on Sunday.

Authorities received a 911 report of a plane crash on the lake at 20:49 local time (02:49 BST), the Marathon County Sheriff's office said in a press release. The pair managed to get out of the plane and to shallow water where a Wausau Fire Department airboat rescued them about 15 minutes later, at 21:05 local time, according to the sheriff's office.
The office said Tiffany and the pilot were the only two people on board the Beechcraft K35 - a single-engine plane, also known as a Bonanza, that can carry up to five people.

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side," Tiffany said. "An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is."
He received a small cut over his right eye in the incident, his campaign said.

The cause of the mechanical issue was not immediately clear, and the sheriff's office said the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the incident.
The plane remains in the lake as emergency crews work to remove it, the office added.

articles.title: Sweden general election: close race as far right eyes role in government – Europe live
articles.summary:
Country heads to the polls as latest polling shows 0.3-point gap between left and right wing blocs

in Stockholm

Hej, that’s…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18m agoHej from Stockholm!
25m agoEvening opening: Welcome to 2026 Swedish parliamentary election live blog

blocks.text: Hej from Stockholm!

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
in Stockholm

Hej, that’s hello in Swedish, from Stockholm, where I spent this morning eating Swedish pastry and meatballs talking to voters about the country’s prospects as they cast their votes in today’s parliamentary elections.
Here is what they told me, straight from Stockholm:
Evening opening: Welcome to 2026 Swedish parliamentary election live blog

We kick off our coverage of the 2026 Swedish parliamentary election which could see the far right enter government for the first time if the country’s rightwing parties can form a majority – or a new centre-left government take control instead.

blocks.caption: Voters take part in Sweden’s general election in the Stockholm region on Sunday. Photograph: Joel Lindhe/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: As our Nordic correspondent Miranda Bryant noted in her preview,

“In 2022, the current prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, the leader of the centre-right Moderates, broke a longstanding taboo to make a deal with the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), so that his minority coalition could form a government. That agreement gave the SD outsized influence over government policy, especially on crime and immigration, and Kristersson has now gone further, promising ministerial posts for the SD if he is returned to power.”

The opposition “red” bloc is led by former prime minister Magdalena ⁠Andersson of the Social Democrats, but their lead has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign to less than one percentage point.
It could be a very, very close race.
The polls opened 8am local time and will close 8pm local time (7pm UK), when we should have two exit polls – conducted by Swedish broadcaster SVT and TV4 – for you.
A further projection will be published by public broadcaster SVT about an hour later, as we start getting actual results.
We could be in for a long night, but hope you will join us for lots of colour from Stockholm, the last hours of the campaign trail, and obviously the results.
Good evening.

articles.title: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists
articles.summary: Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using a family- values campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.

blocks.text: Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.
Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values.
One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL.
Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.
Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office.
In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL.
The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.
It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.

According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.
Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.

As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country.
Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.
However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years.
"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

articles.title: Legendary Canadian boxer George Chuvalo dies aged 89
articles.summary: The heavyweight champion took on the likes of Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier, and was known for never once getting knocked out or knocked down.

blocks.text: "George Chuvalo was a heavyweight boxing legend, a family friend and a Canadian icon," Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media.
"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing."
After retiring from professional boxing in 1978, Chuvalo travelled the country as a public speaker advocating for anti-drug education and mental health awareness.
Chuvalo lost three sons and his wife to drug overdoses and suicide, he has said.

"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family," he once said, according to a CBC Radio report in 1998.
In retirement, Chuvalo also dipped his toes in acting, appearing in the 1998 comedy film Dirty Work and alongside Jeff Goldblum in the 1986 horror film The Fly.
He also served as a guest commentator for major boxing matches and co-hosted a TV boxing program called Greatest Knockouts with his friend and fellow fighter Charles "Spider" Jones.
Chuvalo is survived by his eldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, grandchildren, and second wife Joanne.
He died on Saturday, his birthday, said Sully's Boxing Gym.

articles.title: Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids
articles.summary: Turkish authorities have arrested at least 162 people in a weekend crackdown on the country's LGBTQ+ community. Ankara says police raids on gay bars and other venues are aimed at protecting family…

image.caption: Although same-sex relationships are not illegal in Turkey, the LGBTQ+ community faces harsh repression under the country's authoritarian leader, President Recep Tayyip ErdoganImage: Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Turkish police have arrested at least 162 people and searched the offices of six LGBTQ+ associations in weekend raids designed to support the country's campaign to protect family values.

The Ankara-based LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL claimed that beyond arrests, the government had also cut access to dozens of websites and social media accounts belonging to associate groups and rights advocates.
Government says its fulfilling duty to 'protect families and children'

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigations — prompted by accusations of prostitution and obscenity — were coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin and involved judicial proceedings against 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.

"As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!" Gurlek added in a social media post.

Authorities say they seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a gun in weekend police operations targeting gay bars and night clubs as well as a hammam that was said to be a place of prostitution.
The Istanbul prosecutor's office added that it had found evidence indicating that children and minors were being inappropriately swayed on issues tied to sexual orientation and gender identity.
Rights groups say the government is unfairly targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with Kaos GL saying that it had been accused of making "posts containing obscenities" accessible to children.
Being gay in Turkey
Erdogan scapegoats LGBTQ+ 'perverts' for falling birthrates, avoiding actual contributing factors

The weekend police operation was dubbed "My Family is Safe" by the government and was part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, which is designed to reverse plummeting birthrates in the aging country.

Authorities say it was intended to make sure that society does not see LGBTQ+ activity as "normal" and that raids were carried out to "protect children, the institution of the family, and our shared moral values."
Although same-sex relations are not illegal in the country, homophobia is rife, with President Erdogan blaming LGBTQ "perverts" for Turkey's rapidly declining birthrates.

That would seem a rhetorical diversion from the actual complexity of reasons for the decline, which Erdogan — who has ruled as the country's authoritarian president since 2014 as well as serving as its influential prime minister for 10 years before that — has called "a disaster."

Though Turkey's statistical agency, TurkStat, tracked a sharp decline in the total fertility rate between 2013 and 2023 (from 2.11 to 1.51 ), the shift brings birthrates in the country closer to those in other developed nations.
Observers say the real reasons for the drop are more likely of a structural and institutional nature rather than one chalked up to lifestyle.

Turkey's chronically worsening financial crisis, inflation, skyrocketing housing prices, family unfriendly workplace environments, limited access to affordable childcare, and higher educational and employment rates for women are all considered reasons for Turks to postpone having children, as well as for having fewer when they finally do.

articles.title: World's tallest totem pole comes down in Alert Bay, B.C., after more than 50 years
articles.summary: The world’s tallest totem pole was brought down this week in Alert Bay, B.C., a community off the coast of northeast Vancouver Island. For two 'Na̱mǥis chiefs, the pole — recognized in the Guinness…

image.caption: Due to structural safety concerns, the totem pole in Alert Bay, B.C., was brought down on Sept. 9, 2026. (Submitted by Hazel Cook)

blocks.text: British Columbia

The world’s tallest totem pole was brought down this week in Alert Bay, B.C., a community off the coast of northeast Vancouver Island. For two 'Na̱mǥis chiefs, the pole — recognized in the Guinness Book of World Records — represented much more than its height.
Emotional day as the tallest totem pole in the world, representing unity between tribes, comes down
The world’s tallest totem pole was brought down this week in Alert Bay, B.C., a community off the coast of northeast Vancouver Island.
For two 'Na̱mǥis chiefs, the pole — recognized in the Guinness Book of World Records — represented much more than its height.
"This pole was so much more," said Ho’miskanis Don Svanvik, hereditary chief and elected chief councillor of the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation.
"It was a beacon for our people coming out of a pretty dark time in history," he said, referencing the potlatch ban — the federal law that outlawed potlatching on the coast for more than 60 years.
Svanvik said his great-grandparents were jailed in the 1920s for taking part in potlatch.
"The pole, in some ways, represents people being who they always have been and continue to be," he said.

items: Mi'kmaw mask carver wins Canadian Crafts Federation award
Members of Okanagan Indian Band mourn loss of forests and irreplaceable artifacts in wildfire

blocks.text: "This is who we are. This is how we govern ourselves. This is how we celebrate and acknowledge things, through our ceremonies … this was a time when that was all coming back, coming into the forefront of things."

Crews began dismantling the 173-foot pole on Wednesday in a carefully staged, multi-hour process, after the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation confirmed the structure had become too unstable and hazardous to remain standing.
The nearby Gukwdzi (Big House) and its surrounding parking area were closed the evening before to establish a safety perimeter, and community members gathered nearby to witness.
Nothing lasts forever
The original pole was raised in 1973. It was one tree spliced into two connected sections, according to 'Na̱mǥis Hereditary Chief William Wasden Jr.
He said the pole was designed to carry the crests of 22 Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw tribes — a deliberate statement of unity.
Tribes have amalgamated since then, Wasden said, but it was a powerful symbol of solidarity, an essential theme of the times.
"Our Big House was finished around then too … it was the same theme … somewhere for everybody to come and utilize," Wasden Jr. said.

"Alert Bay was like Grand Central Station, it was almost like the center of Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw territories physically, but people were amalgamating there and so it almost became Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw central."
When the pole came down, Wasden said he felt proud.
"Nothing lasts forever, especially the cedar tree," he said, sharing a story of an ancestor who recognized in ancient times that neither a cedar tree nor a mountain would always stand.
For Wasden, the pole’s takedown is part of a much older pattern, one where each generation is left to answer for itself.
"It’s our ancestors challenging us now," he said. "Are you gonna ride on our coattails, or will you be as great as we were, by doing the things you need to do to uplift your people?"
The pole was carved by a number of carvers at the time, overseen by Jimmy Dick.
Wasden named Jimmy Dick’s son "Blackie," Ben Dick Senior, as the main carver. He named other carvers like Adam Dick, Andy "Beanie" Beans, Gus Matilpi and Dick Dawson.
Svanvik named Henry Hunt and Henry Speck, along with others who may have dropped in at the time.
LISTEN | The day the totem pole was taken down:
All Points West9:10World's tallest totem pole comes down
Both acknowledged Dora Cook who learned to carve alongside the men, one of very few women to do so at the time.
"She was ahead of her time," said Wasden.
Both Wasden and Svanvik remember the pole being carved when they were kids.

Svanvik jokingly said he played a small role when he was called over by the carvers to "squirt oil on the saw" they were using. Wasden carries a photo of himself and his friends sitting on the pole before it was raised.
Both said they look forward to what’s next.
"This is not the end of anything," Svanvik said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emilee Gilpin is an associate producer and reporter for CBC Victoria. You can email her at emilee.gilpin@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials accused Russia of a "systemic attack" on its railways following drone strikes near the Polish border, including a hit on a locomotive of a passenger train headed to Warsaw.

image.caption: No casualties were reported following the drone strikes near PolandImage: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, very near its border with NATO member Poland, Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday.
One of the drones hit a passenger train locomotive in Volyn, some two kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing.
"The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post.
Putin rejects Zelenskyy's G20 talks offer
The company later said that a "systemic attack" was happening throughout Ukraine.
Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory.
"The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw."
Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned'
On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned" and a gas station damaged in Volyn.
"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said.
Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports.

blocks.caption: Falling debris set a gas station on fire near the border checkpoint in VolynImage: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border.
The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid.
'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister
Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."
"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X.

He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex."
"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added.

articles.title: Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
articles.summary: Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany, and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their…

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut in Moscow is one of three branches of Germany’s cultural center that'll have to closeImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany's Goethe-Institut is set toclose all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

blocks.caption: The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 eitherImage: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

blocks.caption: Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

articles.title: Iran war reshapes Brics ties but also exposes divisions
articles.summary: Brics members agree they need a new global order but it's harder to answer what should replace it and how to get there.

blocks.text: This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers".

Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.
These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations.

India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies.

The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war.
But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit.
The summit succeeded in delivering a joint declaration when divisions among members have rarely been so glaring.

Twice earlier this year, meetings between Brics ministers had failed to produce a joint statement. This time a consensus was reached, but by side-stepping issues that members sharply disagree on, with few solutions.
The "New Delhi Declaration" was adopted on the first day of the summit. But what is striking is what it doesn't say.
On the war in the Middle East, the declaration urges "maximum restraint". It also condemns "attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities" but assigns no blame.

It reiterates support for a two-state solution, opposes forced displacement of Palestinians or actions that could "legitimise or prolong occupation", framing it carefully around existing UN resolutions.
It makes no mention at all of Russia's war in Ukraine, a departure from previous Brics declarations.
There is similar caution on trade. It lists concerns over "indiscriminate rising tariffs" and condemns unilateral sanctions but stops short of naming the US, and is likely to avoid Washington's ire.

items: Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi

blocks.text: Several Brics members would have been loath to draw President Donald Trump's anger, as he has previously called the group's proposals, including potentially linking central-bank digital currencies for cross-border trade, "anti-American".
"Not mentioning any country by name, even as they condemned the conflict in the Middle East, bears the hallmark of India," says Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

"I was pleasantly surprised that there was a strong reference to tariffs, because India could have wanted to be less direct about it, but perhaps this was a chance to convey their displeasure," he added.
In the wake of Trump's trade threats and the shock of the war in the Middle East, reshaping the global order has become a vital need for many member economies.
What the summit did provide is a platform for meetings that seemed hard to imagine just a few months ago.
Iran's Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince sat down for talks together - the highest-level face-to-face meeting known between the two countries since the war began.
This weekend offered Tehran a chance to show that it does not stand alone amid the US and Israel's military attacks and economic pressure.

As Iran tries to withstand US sanctions, Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" and a naval blockade on its ports, Pezeshkian pressed for deeper economic ties with Brics members, including Malaysia, India and Ethiopia.

As for China, this was President Xi's first visit to Delhi in seven years. There has been deep mistrust between China and India since the 2020 border dispute, but those tensions have eased. There is also a large trade imbalance, with a deficit tilting heavily in China's favour.
There was a cordial handshake between Xi and Modi, not the latter's signature hug. Xi also stayed for less than 24 hours, skipping the gala dinner hosted by Modi on Saturday night.

But the weekend was still a big moment for two countries with such a difficult relationship. According to official readouts, the two leaders agreed to strengthen business ties and transport links and address barriers to trade.

Trigunayat believes this is part of a gradual warming of relations in recent years, and that there is a will on both sides to work together. But whether it will produce substantial progress remains to be seen.
"I always say we have to trust, but verify first," he says.

articles.title: Voting under way in Sweden with far-right eyeing first role in government
articles.summary:
Party with neo-Nazi roots is in line for key ministerial positions if rightwing bloc wins the election

Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the…

blocks.text: Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) entering government for the first time.

It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Polls suggest an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.
Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (07.00 BST). A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting.

Early indications of results will come at 8pm when the first exit polls are released, followed by a forecast from the broadcaster SVT an hour later. The first preliminary vote count is expected between 10.30 and 11pm. Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.

The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.
The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.

blocks.caption: The leader of the Social Democrats, Magdalena Andersson, casts her vote in Stockholm. Photograph: Stefan Jerrevang/EPA

blocks.text: The rightwing coalition broke a long-standing taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.
SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.

After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition win, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.

SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Their controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.
after newsletter promotion
The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader, Magdalena Andersson, why she was so angry during a TV debate.

Another leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.
Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.

“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”

Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.

The prime minister and leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson, has put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused Andersson of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.

Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”

articles.title: Albertans to vote on opting out of federal programs — while keeping cash
articles.summary: When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration. One of four constitutional questions will ask voters if they support a push to amend the…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith arrives ahead of the First Ministers' Meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Charlottetown on July 23. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary

When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration. One of four constitutional questions will ask voters if they support a push to amend the Constitution so Alberta can opt out of federal programs, while keeping the cash.
It’s 1 of 4 constitutional questions on October ballot, but ‘yes’ vote alone can’t change this
When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration.
Albertans will also be presented with four constitutional questions that range from abolishing the Senate to whether Alberta should appoint the judges who sit on the province’s higher courts.
Third on the list will be a question tied to federal programs like pharmacare. The federal government provides funding to provinces for these programs, sometimes with conditions attached.
The Alberta government wants that to change.
As part of the referendum, voters will be asked if they support a government push to try to amend the Constitution.

The stated goal? To allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services” without losing any associated federal funding for use in social programs.
“What Alberta is gunning for here is an attempt to limit what we call the constitutional spending power,” said Geoffrey Sigalet, director of the UBC Research Group for Constitutional Law.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Power of the purse
By constitutional spending power, Sigalet is referring to Ottawa’s ability to transfer money to provinces and attach conditions to it.
Today, provinces can decline federal funding if they don’t agree with the conditions attached.
But if agreements between provinces and the federal government aren’t reached, that can also mean leaving money on the table, which can be politically unpopular.
“Different constitutional scholars take different perspectives on this,” Sigalet said.
“Some will be more in favour of centralizing this kind of thing. … My own sense is that Alberta has a point here.”
In Sigalet’s view, setting conditions on federal funding sent to other levels of government can look a lot like policymaking in another's jurisdiction.
He noted that some scholars have argued that the spending power is unconstitutional, and others have said it could be open to future litigation.
David Schneiderman, a law professor at the University of Toronto, argued the federal government only oversteps, constitutionally speaking, when it “imposes" programs.
“When it attaches conditions to spending in an area of provincial jurisdiction, a province can simply refuse to accept federal money,” Schneiderman wrote in an email.

“Note that there has not been any serious constitutional challenge to the exercise of the modern federal spending power. Provinces prefer to accept the money — and then erode conditions, as in the case of healthcare.”
This isn’t the first time the federal government’s spending power has been debated.
Not a new debate

The Meech Lake Accord in the 1980s was a failed attempt to amend the Canadian Constitution. One of the proposed amendments was allowing provinces to opt out with "reasonable compensation" of national shared-cost federal programs — with a notable condition.
“Under the language of Meech Lake, it was still a little limiting,” Sigalet said.
Under Meech, provinces could opt out if they established a program compatible with national objectives.
Alberta’s referendum doesn’t mention such a condition. Voters will simply be asked whether they endorse Alberta pursuing a constitutional change.
That change, as the province sees it, would allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.”
But as for then setting up a comparable program?
“We won’t make assumptions about the outcome or what decisions should follow until Albertans have had their say,” wrote Kyle Warner, a spokesperson for the province, in an email.
Schneiderman sees an issue.
“Alberta could negotiate with the feds. It is hard to see any federal government agreeing to something short of the Meech formulation,” he said.
Much like the other constitutional questions on the ballot this October, a “yes” vote doesn’t mean immediate change.
Developing an opt-out rule, in whatever form it might take, would require the support of Parliament, as well as at least seven provinces representing at least half of Canada’s population.
Impact on federal programs
All of this might sound familiar to Albertans.
For instance, take Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s statement in 2024 that the province would pull out of the Canadian Dental Care Plan by 2026.

There are, of course, less than four months to go in the calendar year, and Alberta has yet to exit that plan. A spokesperson for the provincial government said officials continue to work with Ottawa to ensure the province “receives its fair share” of federal funding to further expand its coverage.

items: Why Alberta's government wants out of the federal dental care plan — and who it could impact
Alberta wants to opt out of national pharmacare program

blocks.text: Fiona Clement, director of the Centre for Health Policy at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, said that in her view, the federal government is in charge of a funding method, not a way to deliver the program.
“I would hope if we were standing something up in Alberta on its own, we would also be attracted to concepts like universality and comprehensiveness,” Clement said.

“On a general stand, I think many of the things that are done by the federal government, you are stronger together … there’s a lot of these processes that make a lot of sense to do at the national, federal level.”
The debate around how this money is spent has been going on for decades.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will have the opportunity to weigh in on whether they feel the current arrangement is working, or whether they think Alberta should fight to try to take control of those dollars — no strings attached.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
articles.summary: A rapidly spreading wildfire threatened homes and tourist accommodations on the Croatian island of Brac, with firefighters battling the blaze overnight.

image.caption: The fire spread through remote parts of the island before threatening populated coastal areasImage: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.
The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.
"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."

blocks.caption: Over 220 firefighters and 69 vehicles fought the blaze overnightImage: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.
Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.
"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.
No deaths reported in blaze
Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.

No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.
Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.
Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.
Firefighting planes active on the scene

As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.

blocks.caption: The blaze on the island of Brac was visible from Croatia's second city, SplitImage: Zvonimir Barisin/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.

articles.title: Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
articles.summary: A recent spate of stark warnings about the dangers of AI has been met with scepticism by executives and investors.

blocks.text: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.
This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.
Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.
They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post.
"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.

While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.
Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".
One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".
He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology.
"It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said.

"Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"
Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.
The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.
In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.
Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".

And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.
Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector.
Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole".

On Friday, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety.

"Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety.
Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei.

Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development.

"There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could."
"When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added.

If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China.

Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now."

But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal.
David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic.

OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership".
The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment.
At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI.
OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn, has previously announced plans to allow people to buy shares in its firm by listing on the stock market.

However, its chief executive Sam Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, calling it an "ill-advised moment" to do so "given everything happening with safety" in an interview with Fortune magazine.
He suggested 2027 would be more likely.
Meanwhile, one investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares.
His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable?
When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - CEO of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words.
"No," he said.

articles.title: A Romani artist in Hungary reclaims his identity
articles.summary: Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he avoided making his ethnic background a theme of his art for fear of being pigeonholed. Then it became his focus.

image.caption: Roma artist Norbert Olah in the Bura Galeria in BudapestImage: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

blocks.text: The painting on the canvas is of a man playing chess with a robot. The color on his face is still damp and glistening. Norbert Olah was working into the early hours: The Bura Galeria in Budapest has been his studio all summer. He finds it easiest to concentrate at night, when the Hungarian capital gradually falls silent.

Olah has taped foil and cardboard over the tiled floor at the back of the gallery. Pots of brushes, tubes of paint, pencil sketches, and, over and over again, pictures that include the blue-and-green Roma flag line the room.

Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he deliberately left this part of his identity out of his art. Not because his ethnicity wasn't important to him, but because he didn't want to be labeled a "Romani artist."
"There are so many prejudices about Roma culture and Roma art," Olah says. "The art scene regards it as naïve, unprofessional, unsophisticated, and kitsch."
But the older Olah got, the harder he found it to ignore his own story in his art. Especially in a country in which being Romani is not just an ethnicity but a political reality.
Life under Orban

The first time Viktor Orban's Fidesz party won an absolute majority in the Hungarian parliamentary elections of 2010, Olah had just finished school and was starting his art course at the Hungarian University of Fine Arts in Budapest. At a time of life when the world ought to be opening up, Olah felt more and more barriers were being erected.

blocks.caption: Norbert Olah with his paintings: The Bura Galeria is a platform for contemporary Roma artImage: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

blocks.text: Olah was directly affected by Hungary's political reorientation, as both an artist and a Romani. Politics co-opted the cultural scene and made it toe the party line. Roma became the target of hateful rhetoric, including from the prime minister himself. Orban repeatedly called attention to himself with racist comments about Roma.

For the 16 years Orban was in power, Hungary's Roma population, estimated to be around 700,000 people, was caught between official promises of integration and persistent marginalization. Orban's government introduced a state employment program that hired predominantly Romani workers. But instead of helping them gain a foothold in the job market, many Romani found themselves trapped in insecure, poorly paid, temporary jobs. The government did little to implement real change. Romani in Hungary are still disproportionately affected by poverty and social exclusion.
There came a point when Norbert Olah felt he could no longer stand by and do nothing.
Other people's prejudices

In 2021, during Hungary's biggest independent contemporary art event, the OFF-Biennale Budapest, Olah and his father laid a brick wall directly in front of the entrance to the building that had housed the Roma Parliament, a Roma cultural center with an art collection, archive, library, and events program. The Orban government evicted it in 2016, saying the building was structurally dangerous and promising to repurpose it as a national Roma center. It has stood empty ever since.

The title of Olah's work was "The Romani Artist's Fears." Words like "integration," "assimilation," and "segregation" were chiseled into the bricks. A few weeks later, Olah staged a performance in which he took a sledgehammer to his artwork and smashed it till it collapsed.

In an accompanying text, Olah wrote publicly for the first time about the fears, prejudices, and expectations he encounters as an artist with Roma roots. The text is full of questions. Should a Romani artist's work focus on topics relevant to Roma? What is the relationship between ethnicity and aesthetics? Would people only contact an artist with Roma roots if they were specifically looking for a Romani artist, or would they do so if they needed a Hungarian artist, too?

blocks.caption: Roma on the moon: Olah's current project looks to the futureImage: Norbert Oláh

blocks.text: "Of course we're always looking for answers. But sometimes it's more interesting to look at the question itself," says Olah, picking a piece of crepe masking tape off the floor. "If it feels uncomfortable, it's a good question."

And so Olah has created a new label for Romani artists. The Bura Galeria, established by Romani activists in 2021 in Budapest's District 8, has become the place for it: A platform for contemporary Roma art.
"We're not asking to be accepted by the art scene," said Olah. "We're opening the door and inviting others in."
Open antiziganism
Identity and exclusion, power and the misuse of power — these became central themes for Olah's artistic work. He had no lack of inspiration during the Orban years.

Although Fidesz's policies were hardly favorable to Roma, Orban's party could, for a long time, count on Roma votes — for example, because local employment programs enabled local politicians to pressure socially underprivileged voters. There were also many documented cases of vote-buying. Fidesz was so confident that the majority of Roma would continue to vote for it that it openly fueled the antiziganism still widespread in Hungarian society.
After Orban, Hungary's Roma hope for change

Shortly before the election in April 2026, Fidesz's Janos Lazar, who was minister for transport at the time, spoke out against labor migration with the argument that Hungary still had "domestic reserves," like the Roma, who could "clean the crap out of overflowing toilets" on Intercity trains. The scene appears in Olah's art: A fake election poster depicts a man in a balaclava sitting on a golden toilet, brandishing a toilet brush, with the slogan underneath: "Gypsy Criminals for President."
Opportunity for real change?

Gypsy Criminals is also the name of the artists' collective Olah founded in 2024, along with a friend of his and his miniature pinscher. The term comes from Hungarian crime statistics, and has been used since the 2000s by right-wing politicians to imply that all Roma are criminals. The name is ironic, like many aspects of Olah's work.

Analyses by the foundation Roma for Democracy show that many Roma did not vote for Orban's Fidesz party in the April 2026 parliamentary election. Orban's successor, Peter Magyar, adopted a different tone in relation to Roma as part of his election campaign. He met with members of the Roma minority, and his election manifesto contained a specific paragraph about equal opportunities for Roma. Four of the Tisza party's nine new members of parliament are Romani. One was even elected a deputy speaker of parliament.

Since the election, there has been cautious optimism that the precarious situation of many Roma in Hungary could finally change. On the other hand, nothing has fundamentally changed in the four months since the election, apart from the tone when talking about the ethnic minority. "What I'm seeing right now are mostly symbolic gestures," says Olah.
Roma on Mars
Some of his friends in the more liberal art scene are growing impatient. They would like to see Magyar take a much more liberal course, but Olah is a realist.

"He's a conservative politician," he says. "We elected him to put an end to the Orban system. He didn't promise any more than that." But the election in April was an opportunity for a fresh political start, he adds. "I think in the long run we will live in a normal society again, led by a normal government, that will do some things well and others not so well. As an artist, it will be my job to criticize that."

blocks.caption: Man v. robot: Olah works on a new painting in his Budapest studioImage: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

blocks.text: Olah's work also considers the future. The first pictures for his next project are already up on the wall in his studio. It's Roma futurism: A Romani couple strolling on Mars; a blue-and-green Roma flag on the moon; a weightless astronaut with a traditional Cegled water jug, used by Romani musicians as a percussion instrument. Olah is also planning a two-meter-high space station in the shape of a cartwheel, a symbol of the Romani people.

For Olah, space travel is also a metaphor for social advancement — the desire of people and communities to overcome the barriers they face as a result of their origins, or poverty, or life in a minority. Again, he is asking questions. What if a society were fundamentally recreated from the beginning? If aliens encountered Roma, would they do so without prejudice? What remains of an identity if everything about it changes?
Olah shreds the masking tape between his fingers. More unanswered questions. But that's exactly what makes them so interesting.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Beauty can be made. Yet ‘natural beauty’ still matters in Korea
articles.summary: Can a beauty pageant title be considered any less authentic if the winner’s appearance has been surgically enhanced? The question emerged after earlier images of this year’s Miss Korea, Woo Seo-yoon,…

blocks.text: Can a beauty pageant title be considered any less authentic if the winner’s appearance has been surgically enhanced?
The question emerged after earlier images of this year’s Miss Korea, Woo Seo-yoon, began circulating online following her crowning at the 70th Miss Korea pageant on Aug. 22.

The images prompted comparisons with her current appearance and speculation about what, if anything, she may have done to change her looks. Some argued that Miss Korea should favor contestants with no history of cosmetic procedures. Others noted that the pageant does not prohibit surgery and questioned the scrutiny of Woo based on old photographs.
Woo, 22, herself did not address the issue directly. She said, however, that the negativity and hateful comments were “hurtful” and that she was determined not to let them affect her.
“I hope I will have opportunities to show people who I really am,” she said in an interview.
Woo is not the first Miss Korea winner to face scrutiny after earlier photographs surfaced online.
Jung Yeon-woo, who won the title last year, said that questions about cosmetic surgery were among the comments she heard most often during her time as Miss Korea.

“Time and again, I’ve watched people hurt not only me but also colleagues I care about with such rude and hurtful remarks,” she said on Instagram in response to questions about whether she was a “natural beauty.”

“I’m more curious about why people are so curious about whether someone has had plastic surgery,” she added. “Does being a natural beauty make you more valuable, and does not being one make you less so?”
‘Natural beauty’
Jung’s question points to a larger contradiction in Korean beauty culture.

In a country where enhancing the looks people are born with — through skincare, makeup, styling, cosmetic treatments or even surgery — has become deeply woven into everyday culture and helped fuel a lucrative beauty industry with global reach, why are people still so fixated on the idea of natural beauty?
Even the meaning of a “natural look” has become blurred.

In Korea, looking natural does not necessarily mean going without makeup or cosmetic treatments. Instead, it often refers to an aesthetic designed to look effortlessly attractive — one that, paradoxically, can require considerable time, skillful makeup and careful styling.
Lee Sun-mi, 47, said there’s something about discovering that someone known for being exceptionally beautiful once looked ordinary — like herself.

“When someone is naturally beautiful, they’re just born that way — extraordinary. But when someone becomes beautiful through surgery, I think people feel that they could look the same, but simply chose not to, or didn’t have the means to have surgery,” Lee said.
That logic may help explain why the idea of “natural beauty” remains powerful, particularly in beauty pageants, where the title is still closely associated with physical attractiveness.

“Beauty pageants have traditionally been seen as contests that recognized women with exceptional natural beauty,” said Huh Chang-deog, a sociology professor at Yeungnam University. “That perception continues to shape public expectations, even as cosmetic surgery and other procedures have become increasingly common.”
But the Miss Korea competition, founded in 1957, has changed, seeking to reflect shifting attitudes toward women and beauty and the values of the times.

Today’s contestants are evaluated through interviews, group activities and other stages of the competition, rather than on physical appearance alone. The pageant dropped its swimsuit round in 2019 following criticism that it objectified contestants, and recent competitions have placed greater emphasis on intelligence, social engagement and other qualities.

The 2026 finalists included law school graduates, students at leading universities in Korea and abroad, and women from a range of academic and professional backgrounds. Woo herself studied art at Tufts University.
A senior official at Global E&B, which organizes Miss Korea, told The Korea Herald that whether a contestant has undergone cosmetic surgery or is naturally beautiful has little bearing on judging.

“We assess contestants on both their appearance and personal beauty, including their commitment to social causes and ESG values. These areas are carefully evaluated and carry significant weight. Both are equally important,” the official said, declining to disclose how much weight is given to each category amid the recent controversy.
Huh also emphasized that the debate about natural beauty tends to reduce beauty to something purely physical.

“Someone may not fit conventional beauty standards yet still be attractive because of their demeanor, the warmth of their smile or the empathy they show toward others,” he said. “Beauty takes many forms.” /dl

articles.title: One dead, 102 rescued from Indonesian ferry that went missing in Java Sea
articles.summary: The nation's search and rescue team said it lost contact with the Virgo Transport 8 in the early hours of Sunday morning.

blocks.text: Image source, Donny Muslim / BBC
Families of victims gather at Trisakti Port, Banjarmasin
One person has died and 102 have been rescued from a stricken Indonesian passenger ferry in the Java Sea, an official said.

A search and rescue operation was launched after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 ship, which was carrying 243 people, as it encountered bad weather, Indonesia's search and rescue agency said.
The search for the remaining passengers is ongoing.

The ferry was travelling from Surabaya to the South Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin and was last reported to be about 150km (93 miles) south of Banjarmasin around 02:00 local time on Sunday (18:00 GMT on Saturday).

Authorities received the initial distress report at 04:10 from the vessel's operator PT Virgo. The ship left Surabaya at 10:33 on Saturday and was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin on Sunday at 14:00, according to data from two maritime monitoring sites.
A joint task force involving Indonesia's search and rescue agency, navy, maritime police and other parties has been set up for the rescue effort.
Ships and a helicopter have been deployed to the scene and all other vessels in that area of the Java Sea have been alerted to report signs of any passengers.
An operations post for handling the accident was set up in the Trisakti Port area on Sunday morning.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Indonesian authorities reported the Virgo Transport 8 lost contact in the Java Sea while en route from Surabaya to Banjarmasin

blocks.text: Indonesian authorities reported the Virgo Transport 8 lost contact in the Java Sea while en route from Surabaya to Banjarmasin

Rusmilawati, a resident of Banjarmasin, went to the port to seek information about eight relatives who were passengers on the ship. They were travelling back to Banjarmasin after visiting the tombs of several Islamic scholars in Java.
"They flew there initially, but for the return journey they wanted to try travelling by ship," she said.
As of Sunday afternoon local time, Rusmilawati said she had not received any information from officials about whether her relatives had been rescued.

The family last heard from one of the relatives through a WhatsApp status update. In the post, the relative wrote: "The waves are really frightening tonight. Or is this just what it's normally like travelling by ship, rocking and crashing against the waves?"
"Hopefully they're safe," Rusmilawati said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Family members of the victims wait to hear news about their loved ones at Trisakti Port

blocks.text: Family members of the victims wait to hear news about their loved ones at Trisakti Port
Meanwhile, Misnah broke down in tears after learning that her husband, Ahmad Supandi, had survived.
Ahmad, a freight driver, had been aboard Virgo Transport 8 and was later rescued by the vessel MV Haida.
At Tanjung Perak Port in Surabaya, relatives of crew members have also been seeking information about their loved ones.
One relative, Fredy, said his youngest sibling, Stevie Manuhua, worked aboard the vessel as a keyboard player, entertaining passengers.
"We spoke two days ago when the ship was docked in Surabaya. After that, there was no news until now," Fredy said.
He said he had still not received any information about his sibling's whereabouts.

articles.title: Are electric cars really bad for the environment?
articles.summary: “The EU’s car lie” — Germany’s Bild tabloid newspaper didn’t mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union’s “dangerous” claim that…

blocks.text: “The EU’s car lie” — Germany’s Bild tabloid newspaper didn’t mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union’s “dangerous” claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral.

Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to “the EU’s phaseout of internal combustion engines” set for 2035. Stepping away from the phaseout, he said, would now be backed by “science.”

Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU’s climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered “climate-neutral.”

The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only “41% on average” over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix.

Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle’s entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling.
It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM.
No new insights in TUM report

Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) think tank, said TUM’s analysis didn’t offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known.

Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%.

Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car’s brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don’t match fully electric vehicles.

blocks.caption: Are electric cars really bad for the environment?

blocks.text: Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe.
Batteries have a high environmental cost

Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water.

Bieker’s ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine.

blocks.caption: While lithium-iron phosphate batteries tend to be cheaper and last longer, nickel manganese cobalt batteries deliver more power and work better in colder climatesImage: Rodrigo Freitas/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: “We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production,” Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they’re generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture.

Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans.
Renewable energy making the case for EVs

The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don’t produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas.
But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs.

blocks.caption: Home solar power installations have taken off in Germany, giving EV owners a cheaper way to charge their carsImage: Daniel Reinhardt/IMAGO

blocks.text: “Europe’s electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonized and expected to be almost fully decarbonized by 2040,” said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. “As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will only strengthen the case even more.”

Clark said it wasn’t necessary to replace the EU’s current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules.

“Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector,” she told DW in an email. “Their replacement of [internal combustion engine] vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed.”
Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth
Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy.
