“The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think,” he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia.

blocks.caption: EV sales have increased in Asia in recent years, with China’s BYD leading the packImage: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% of respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns.
“We cannot win the race by ignoring it,” said Bieker. “[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down.” /dl

articles.title: ‘Smitten’ CEO sues ex-girlfriend to recover $468,000 after break-up
articles.summary: SINGAPORE – After breaking up with his girlfriend of more than a year, the chief executive of a listed company sued her to recover the $468,090 he had spent on her during their relationship. On Sept…

blocks.text: SINGAPORE – After breaking up with his girlfriend of more than a year, the chief executive of a listed company sued her to recover the $468,090 he had spent on her during their relationship.
On Sept 9, the Singapore High Court dismissed Chander Agarwal’s claim that the various sums of money he spent on his former girlfriend, Felicia Lee, were loans that had to be repaid.
In a written judgment, Senior Judge Lee Seiu Kin ruled that most of the sums were gifts that Agarwal had willingly given to Lee.
These include $206,000 in credit card charges, $129,000 spent on overseas trips, $17,000 to engage a feng shui master for her flat and $30,000 in fees for a Stanford-NUS executive program.
Agarwal failed to prove he had given her two other sums, including $50,000 he claimed he lent her to clear a debt to her former employer, the judge said.
The judge added that Agarwal could not point to any evidence showing that the woman had requested the disputed sums as loans or had agreed to repay him.
“The evidence before me clearly shows that the claimant, smitten by the defendant, had showered her with expensive gifts during their relationship,” the judge said.
“Unfortunately, when their relationship ended on a sour note, the claimant became embittered and was determined to extract a price from her.”
The judge quoted the lines from the 1697 play The Mourning Bride: “Heav’n has no rage, like love to hatred turn’d, nor hell a fury, like a woman scorn’d.”
He said: “This case shows that such emotion is not the sole province of one gender.”
Agarwal is the CEO and managing director of TCI Express, an Indian company listed on the National Stock Exchange of India and the Bombay Stock Exchange.
The defendant is a former flight attendant who later worked as an insurance agent and medical sales officer.
They met on a flight in 2019. Agarwal later approached Lee on Facebook, and they started meeting up.
In September 2022, they began a romantic relationship, which ended in December 2023 after he suspected her of infidelity.
He filed the lawsuit in March 2024.
Even before the relationship started, he gave her numerous lavish gifts without expecting repayment.

He once booked a limousine to take her home after dinner, bought her luxury items from brands such as Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Prada, and paid almost all her expenses on a European tour they took together.

In May 2021, when she said on WhatsApp that it had been years since she last took a plane, Agarwal replied: “Soon, soon can fly. I have a first class/suite ticket booked for you already, wherever you want to go when it opens. If not, take the private jet then.”
When she messaged him in August 2022 to ask how she could repay him, he replied: “No need. I am not a moneylender.”
In September 2022, he told her she should not be shy about using his money if they were “together” and offered her a monthly budget of $1,500 for taxi, dining and beauty expenses.
In December 2022, he offered her the use of his American Express Centurion Card, telling her in a text message: “You don’t have a budget now. Anything you want.”
Another message said: “And spoil yourself too, please.”
Suspicious circumstances

The judge said: “While it is not uncommon for exchanges between romantic partners to be informal, it is telling that the claimant could not point to, for example, any WhatsApp message where the defendant acknowledged receipt of the loans that she had allegedly requested.”
Agarwal, represented by Mohamed Baiross, presented a handwritten agreement to the court purportedly signed by the woman.
In the document, the woman purportedly stated that the monthly “deposit” of $10,000 to $25,000 she took from Agarwal belonged to him.
The woman, represented by Sunil Singh Panoo, denied having signed or even seen the document before the court proceedings.
The judge said the circumstances in which the agreement was presented were suspect and gave limited weight to a handwriting expert’s opinion that the signature was genuine.

Although Agarwal based his claims purely on the agreement, he made no reference to it in his original statement of claim, which instead stated that he “never insisted that the parties entered into a formal written agreement”.
He referred to the agreement only seven months later, when he filed an amended statement of claim.

The judge also pointed out that the statements in the document were contradicted by the facts. For instance, the woman did not take $10,000 to $25,000 a month but instead received various sums for different purposes from time to time.

In any event, a subsequent note signed by Agarwal in May 2023, in which he promised that he would never ask for the return of items given to her out of goodwill, superseded any prior agreement, the judge said.
Cross-examined during the trial, Agarwal said that when they started dating, “everything became a loan, everything was transactional”, but “before that, it wasn’t”.
He also said that once she accepted his offers to spend his money, the expenses would automatically become loans.
The judge said the stance taken by Agarwal was contrary to common sense and unsustainable.

He added that Agarwal was likely being evasive when confronted in court with unfavourable evidence, such as his repeated offers to the defendant to spend for her benefit and assurances that she did not need to repay him.

The judge also rejected Agarwal’s argument that the woman induced him to give her the disputed sums by making false representations that they were in a genuine and exclusive relationship and that she would repay him.
The judge said Agarwal’s conduct during the relationship appeared to be a continuation of his relationship style before the couple started dating.

This conclusion was supported by evidence showing that Agarwal had sexual relations with other women while the couple were in a relationship, casting doubt on whether he himself considered their relationship to be genuine and exclusive, the judge added. /dl

articles.title: Myanmar seeks closer foreign ties amid global isolation
articles.summary: Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties. There was nothing unusual…

blocks.text: Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a three-day state visit on Sunday to Vietnam, where the Southeast Asian neighbors vowed to boost defense and security ties.

There was nothing unusual about the trip itself, except that it marked the ex-general’s sixth official trip abroad since assuming Myanmar’s presidency in April, when he was voted in by a parliament stacked with loyalists following military-run elections in December and January that were widely considered a charade.

As Myanmar’s newly minted head of state, Min Aung Hlaing has been hosted by the leaders of India, China, Laos, Thailand, Russia and now Vietnam — six countries in five months. He’ll be heading to Cambodia on Friday to make it seven.

“Since the December-January elections and Min Aung Hlaing’s transition to president after giving up his role as commander-in-chief, he’s really put a renewed focus on diplomatic partnership and trying to shore up the government’s allies in the region,” said Hunter Marston, head of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.

“Even if they’re relatively short trips to regional friends and allies, I think it shows that there is an acceleration of Naypyitaw’s strategy to diversify its partnerships and to normalize relations bilaterally,” he added, referring to Myanmar’s capital.
Human rights situation in Myanmar sinks to new low

Marston and other analysts told DW that Myanmar is slowly returning to the international stage, aiming to shed its pariah status despite the mountain of war crimes allegations leveled against the regime — some against Min Aung Hlaing himself.
Since Min Aung Hlaing’s military toppled the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021, civil war has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million.

Last month, the United Nations said human rights conditions in the country had sunk to a new low, as the military keeps up a campaign of forced recruitment, arson and often indiscriminate air strikes on contested and resistance-held areas.

That record has also made Myanmar one of the most heavily sanctioned countries in the world and brought on a number of court filings for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity at The Hague and elsewhere.

Despite that record, “the military regime is emerging to some extent from its isolation, but engagement is still largely limited to countries that were working with it to some extent prior to the recent sham elections,” said Scot Marciel, a senior adviser at the consulting firm BowerGroupAsia.

“The military clearly hopes increased engagement will give it legitimacy that will help it cement its status, but it has not gained any legitimacy among the Myanmar public,” Marciel, a former US ambassador to Myanmar, added.
Divisions in ASEAN over Myanmar
Even among its Southeast Asian neighbors, holdouts remain.

Since the coup, the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which Myanmar is one, has barred Min Aung Hlaing and his foreign ministers from attending the bloc’s most senior-level meetings.

Malaysia, Indonesia and current ASEAN chair, the Philippines, are especially adamant that it stay that way until Myanmar makes meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that all the members agreed to in April 2021.

Myanmar’s regime has made little progress on the plan so far and rejected repeated requests for ASEAN’s special envoys to the country to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi, who was arrested the morning of the coup and has been held in custody since.
Last month, the country’s newly installed parliament passed a motion flatly rejecting the bloc’s peace plan, and its Foreign Ministry said ASEAN’s special envoys were no longer needed.

Under the circumstances, Min Aung Hlaing and his ministers are unlikely to be attending ASEAN’s senior leaders summits “any time soon,” said Pinitbhand Paribatra, an associate professor of international relations at Thailand’s Thammasat University.
Marston and Marciel, though, say there’s a good chance ASEAN will welcome Myanmar fully back into the fold once Thailand assumes the bloc’s rotating, one-year chairmanship in 2028.

With significant business and security interests in Myanmar and a shared border stretching over 2,400 kilometers, Thailand has been keen to placate the country’s regime and to urge the rest of ASEAN to do the same.

Thailand’s premier and foreign minister “have been very clear that they want to pursue calibrated engagement [with Myanmar] and that they have already seen sufficient progress to incentivize further engagement,” said Marston.
Japan willing to restore normal ties?

Beyond China, Russia and Southeast Asia, Marston and Pinitbhand say Myanmar may also find countries to reengage with among Russia’s authoritarian allies in Central Asia and elsewhere. Min Aung Hlaing made visits to Belarus even before he was president.
Among democratic countries, Pinitbhand said Japan was “more than ready” to restore normal relations with Myanmar.

“I don’t think that Min Aung Hlaing will be traveling to Japan any time soon. But … there might be some other attempts from Japan to, for example, resume the relationship, because the Japanese private sector already has lots of investments and everything inside the country,” he said.
Marciel pointed to both Japan and South Korea as countries that might start normalizing their relations with Myanmar in the next year or so.

blocks.caption: The civil war in Myanmar has killed some 100,000 people and displaced over 3 million since 2021 [FILE: August 10, 2024]Image: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Will the West reengage with Myanmar?

As for countries in the West, the analysts say they see little to no chance of them welcoming Min Aung Hlaing and his regime back onto the world stage or of lifting the heavy sanctions they have placed on them.

Pinitbhand says that’s especially true if the International Criminal Court ultimately decides to issue the arrest warrant its former chief prosecutor had asked for against Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity. A decision is still pending.

Marston says it’s possible Washington would go for “calibrated reengagement” with Naypyitaw if it were to release Aung San Suu Kyi and follow up with other reforms, as the administration of former US President Barack Obama did when she was freed from house arrest in 2010.

“But in this case, I don’t think there are the leader-level engagements to begin to have that conversation between Naypyitaw and Washington, or the strategic interest within the Trump administration to do so,” he said.

Marciel also said that Myanmar was low on the Trump administration’s list of priorities. But with human rights also low on that list, he added, there was a chance it would warm to the regime for the right commercial or economic opportunities.
On the whole, though, the former ambassador says the West won’t be embracing Min Aung Hlaing and his regime for now.

“I don’t see any movement to ease sanctions among the Western countries that maintain them, as they all see the recent elections as a sham and also do not give much priority to Myanmar matters in their foreign policy,” he said. “Things could change, but that is how it looks for now.” /dl

articles.title: African Parks: when conservation becomes a question of power
articles.summary: Prince Harry has long been a supporter of African wildlife and nature. When the British royal first became involved with African Parks in 2016, he served as a prominent figure supporting awareness on…

blocks.text: Prince Harry has long been a supporter of African wildlife and nature. When the British royal first became involved with African Parks in 2016, he served as a prominent figure supporting awareness on elephant conservation.
Later, the son of King Charles III became president of the organization before joining its board in 2023.
But reports indicate that in just a few weeks’ time, he will step down from his position at African Parks. The NGO claims that the move is merely part of a reshuffling of its board.

But Dutch journalist and author Olivier van Beemen, who has extensively investigated the South Africa-based wildlife conservation group, believes the association between Harry and African Parks has increasingly become a burden — for both sides.

blocks.caption: Prince Harry served as President of African Parks from 2017 to 2023, before joining its board of directorsImage: Rwanda Presidency/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prince harming? Organization and Harry ‘see each other as a liability’

Harry’s role was to mainly open doors for African Parks, van Beemen says. His fame attracted media attention and helped the NGO gain access to potential donors. But his notorious falling-out with his family increasingly failed to improve the organization’s coffers and image.
At the same time, allegations of human rights abuses at African Parks made the prince’s association with the organization increasingly problematic.

“I think they now see each other more as a liability,” van Beemen told DW, stressing that the full story reaches far beyond a junior member of the royal family simply stepping down from a ribbon-cutting role.
An NGO with state-like powers
According to its own figures, African Parks manages 24 protected areas in 13 African countries, covering more than 20 million hectares. By 2030, the organization aims to manage as many as 30 parks.
Its business model is known as delegated management: African governments hand over the long-term management of protected areas to the group.
The land formally remains state-owned. But the organization takes on wide-ranging responsibilities, including conservation, infrastructure, tourism and anti-poaching operations.

For African governments, this model offers a major advantage: African Parks brings international funding, expertise and personnel to protected areas that many states would otherwise struggle to manage on their own.

blocks.caption: African Parks: when conservation becomes a question of power

blocks.text: In order to achieve its objectives on the ground, African Parks employs a host of armed rangers across the continent, who are allowed to use indelicate methods if and when needed; in some cases, its influence even extends to managing border controls.

“They take over the state’s monopoly on the use of force within the park,” says van Beemen, adding that some critics of the NGO have gone as far as describing African Parks as a “state within a state.”
It is in this context that mounting allegations of human rights abuses have been recorded in recent years, with conservation efforts repeatedly coming into conflict with local communities.
The shadow of the Baka case
The worst allegations of rights abuses emerged in 2023 at Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo.
Members of the indigenous Baka community reported violence, torture and sexual abuse at the hands of African Parks’ rangers.

The NGO subsequently commissioned the London-based firm Omnia Strategy to investigate the allegations, resulting in African Parks eventually acknowledging certain instances of human rights abuses two years later — though the full investigation report was never made public.

According to van Beemen, the report was not even shown to the government of the Republic of Congo, despite African Parks operating there under an agreement with the government. To this day, it remains unclear what exactly happened in Odzala-Kokoua, and how many people were affected.

African Parks has promised reforms while conceding past failures in its own systems and processes; still, it has remained highly intransparent about the details involved in the entire scandal, says van Beemen.

blocks.caption: Dutch journalist Olivier van Beemen visited numerous wildlife reserves run by African Parks, including the Majete Wildlife Reserve in MalawiImage: privat

blocks.text: Division over findings in Dutch book

The Dutch journalist has meanwhile published a book on the whole affair, titled “Beasts and Men.” The volume won several awards in the Netherlands and has attracted international attention and acclaim.

However, African Parks fundamentally rejects van Beemen’s portrayal of the organization, saying his book contains “hundreds of factual inaccuracies” as well as “a similar number of deeply misleading statements.”
Regarding the human rights abuse allegations, African Parks says some of the cases described by van Beemen had occurred outside the NGOs control.

At the same time, it stressed in a statement that it has a zero-tolerance policy toward abuse, and that there is training in place on human rights standards as well as a comprehensive complaints mechanism for transgressions.

blocks.caption: Armed rangers patrol areas managed by African Parks, including some national bordersImage: DW

blocks.text: But as part of his research, van Beemen also spoke to several former rangers and people affected by conservation operations in several African countries, where he says he repeatedly encountered a fundamental problem perpetuated by African Parks: the loose definition of what constitutes poaching.

According to the accounts he collected, the NGO also treats some locals who hunt animals for their own consumption as poachers, rather than using that term exclusively to describe professional poachers who kill rhinos or elephants for international criminal networks.
Van Beemen said that during his research in Zambia, former rangers told him about the brutal treatment the people taken into custody on such grounds can face.
“This can involve beatings. It can involve very serious torture,” he told DW.
Hiding behind a colonial mindset?

The history of African Parks is also controversial. The organization was founded by Dutch businessman Paul Fentener van Vlissingen, who — according to van Beemen — reportedly held Africans in low regard.
Among other things, he refused to accept the international economic sanctions against the South African apartheid system during the 1980s.

A former close associate of the founder told the Dutch journalist that at the top echolons of the organization, Africans were allegedly considered incapable of protecting their own natural resources because they lacked the money and management skills to do so.

blocks.caption: Anti-poaching initiatives are among the many responsibilities covered by the NGO. In order to make them uninteresting for poachers, many rhinos have their horns removedImage: Mujahid Safodien/AFP

blocks.text: In its early years, African Parks was headquartered in the Netherlands where according to van Beemen, employees would routinely look at maps of Africa and plan where the organization could take over additional parks.
“For me, it was very difficult not to think of the colonialists of earlier centuries looking at the same maps and searching for opportunities for colonial expansion,” van Beemen told DW.

African Parks meanwhile has also rejected this particular characterization of its ethos, pointing at the many relevant contracts it has signed with African governments in good faith and with mutual respect.
Conservation and accountability

The scandal meanwhile also hits closer to Europe not only because of Prince Harry’s departure from the NGO, but also due to the fact that European and German funding also goes to projects involving African Parks.
The organization stresses that these funds enable it to enter cooperations with local communities, which African Parks claims are increasingly at the heart of its work.

The organization says that there are local people living in 64% of the areas where it manages wildlife and nature, while legal access to resources is allowed in 90% of the parks. Only four of the 23 parks are fully fenced, it adds.
But without sufficient scrutiny and accountability, there is no way of verifying the details behind those claims. /dl

articles.title: Vanuatu: One dead, 30 missing after ferry sinks
articles.summary: SYDNEY — One person died and 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the South Pacific nation’s government said on Sunday. The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail on Friday…

blocks.text: SYDNEY — One person died and 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the South Pacific nation’s government said on Sunday.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail on Friday with more than 40 passengers and crew from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones. Search and rescue operations are continuing,” read a statement from Vanuatu Prime Minister Jotham Napat’s office on Sunday.
Fifteen of those onboard have been “accounted for alive” and one dead body has been recovered, the statement said.
“Over 30 people remain missing at sea,” it said.
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Noumea, New Caledonia said it is assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
The member of parliament for Luganville, Matai Seremaiah, who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the southeast coast where currents may have carried survivors. /dl

articles.title: Stricken ferry off Indonesia’s Java: One dead, 102 rescued
articles.summary: JAKARTA — One person was killed and more than 100 were rescued on Sunday after a ferry sailing between the Indonesian islands of Java and Borneo was hit by bad weather, rescue officials said.…

blocks.text: JAKARTA — One person was killed and more than 100 were rescued on Sunday after a ferry sailing between the Indonesian islands of Java and Borneo was hit by bad weather, rescue officials said.
The Virgo Transport 8, carrying 243 passengers and crew, had lost contact with its shipping company early on Sunday after departing from Surabaya in East Java.
“We can inform you that the total number of evacuated passengers is 103 people,” local search and rescue chief I Putu Sudayana said.
One of the passengers had died, he told reporters in the port city of Banjarmasin, where the vessel was headed.
Rescuers battled waves of up to 2.5 metres (8.2 feet) to reach the ferry, he added.
“It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 meters long, is at great risk,” he said, referring to Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency.
Sudayana earlier told AFP that the ship’s captain had reported that the vessel was “tilting” before losing contact.
The vessel’s last position had been detected in the Java Sea, around 150 kilometres (90 miles) from its destination.
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia — an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are the main reasons for the disasters.

On Monday, a speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists working for local and international news agencies went missing near a volcano, Mount Anak Krakatau, in Banten province and a search is ongoing.
The journalists were sent to cover the volcano’s eruption that paralysed Jakarta’s main airport and several others.
Last month, a fire on board a ferry killed one person and left five others missing while 211 were rescued in the Lombok Strait off Indonesia’s Bali island.
The ferry had been heading from Bali to Lombok when it ran into trouble in the early hours of August 12.
In July, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small island south of Sulawesi. /dl

articles.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
articles.summary: Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen’s internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone…

blocks.text: Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen’s internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen’s government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.
The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.

The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran’s. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.

“This is actually a full-scale war,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. “It hasn’t been given that name yet but we are marching there full time,” Al-Muslimi said.
Houthis ‘much stronger’

The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen’s government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.

The Houthis control Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and most of the country’s north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

blocks.caption: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict

blocks.text: The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen’s joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.

Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. “The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger,” Manea said, “while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented.”
What’s Pakistan’s role?

Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen’s ousted government. “Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it,” Manea said.

The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.
“At present, I consider the second scenario more likely,” Manea said.
Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: “The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost.”

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.

Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. “But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out,” Gower said. “Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran,” she added, “and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation.”

blocks.caption: Thousands of civilians fled their homes this week, while nearly 200 were killed in the fighting, according to international bodiesImage: AFP

blocks.text: Humanitarian toll rises
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the “harsh reality” of a return to war.

The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen’s conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.

The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warnedthat around 18,500 people have been displaced. “Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it’s safe to go back,” Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen’s chief of mission, said in a statement. “Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before,” he said. “Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild.”

This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. “When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost,” she said.

“Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life,” she said. “The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war,” she added. /dl

articles.title: iSON Group commits fresh $75-M outlay for PH expansion, more jobs
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — An Indian conglomerate is investing $75 million (P4.7 billion) in new and expanded Philippine operations expected to generate about 2,000 jobs, as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — An Indian conglomerate is investing $75 million (P4.7 billion) in new and expanded Philippine operations expected to generate about 2,000 jobs, as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. sought to attract more investments during his visit to India.

The commitment from iSON Group covers agricultural technology, healthcare, business process outsourcing (BPO) and digital infrastructure, Trade Secretary Maria Cristina Roque said, according to a statement issued by the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) on Sunday.
The investment includes a proposed $50-million agro-solar project, healthcare and 24/7 teleconsultation services, and a $10-million expansion of BPO and global delivery centers.
Roque said iSON’s planned investments aligned with the administration’s priorities, particularly food security and the expansion of digital services.
“They want to improve technology in the agriculture sector,” Roque said after Marcos’ meetings with Indian business executives at the Taj Mahal Hotel in New Delhi on Saturday.
“Agriculture and food security are among the main priorities of the president, so any advancement in agricultural technology is important to the country,” she added.

President Marcos is in India for a two-day visit to attend the 18th BRICS Summit, where he is expected to hold a bilateral meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He was invited to the summit in his capacity as chairman of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
The proposed teleconsultation service could also help address the shortage of healthcare access in remote and geographically isolated communities, Roque said.
The service is expected to cost about P65 a month and would allow patients to consult doctors online at any time, although final implementation details have yet to be determined.
“We are a country of 7,600 islands, so sometimes it is difficult to consult a doctor, especially when the nearest facility is in another town,” Roque said.
The planned expansion would add to iSON Group’s existing Philippine operations.
Its digital infrastructure arm, iSON Tower Ltd. Inc., has operated in the country since 2021 under the Department of Information and Communications Technology’s Common Tower Policy.
The company has invested around $65 million in the Philippines and deployed about 450 telecommunications towers serving approximately 600 tenants across Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.
In August, iSON said it is planning to invest $250 million in agricultural and solar projects in addition to its ongoing $300-million telecommunications tower rollout. /dl

articles.title: Indonesian rescue crews searching for 140 people after ferry hit bad weather
articles.summary:
More than 100 others on board were evacuated from the Virgo ⁠Transport 8 ship, including one who died

Indonesian rescuers were searching on Sunday for 140 people from a ⁠passenger ship that…

blocks.text: Indonesian rescuers were searching on Sunday for 140 people from a ⁠passenger ship that was earlier reported missing in the Java Sea ​after 103 others were evacuated, ‌one of whom ‌died, a search and rescue agency official said.
A passenger ship carrying more than 240 people was reported missing after losing contact during bad weather in the Java Sea early on Sunday, the country’s ⁠search and rescue agency said.
The Virgo ⁠Transport 8 ship set sail ​on Saturday from ‌the East Java ‌city of Surabaya to the South ‌Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin before losing contact.
I Putu Sudayana, the head of the agency’s Banjarmasin office, ​said in a video statement that 103 people had been evacuated using different ships and some of them would be taken to an East Java port.
Rescuers launched a search, deploying a ⁠team, ships and a helicopter toward the passenger vessel’s last ​known position, ​he said, without stating what happened ​to the ship.

The search and rescue office in the city of Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan, which is located on Borneo island, said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 at about 2am on Sunday.

“The ship’s operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather,” Sudayana, who heads the search and rescue office, said in a video briefing.
Indonesia, an archipelago of 17,000 islands, relies ⁠heavily on ferries as a key mode ​of ​transportation, with sea ​routes more affordable and readily ​available than ‌air travel.
However, ​safety ​standards are not always rigorously enforced, resulting in a relatively high accident rate.
This is a developing story

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11: Al-Qaeda weakened but not gone
articles.summary: The extremist preacher Abdullah al-Muhaysini no longer has to worry about US sanctions. In late August 2026, the US Department of the Treasury removed the former jihadist from the Specially…

blocks.text: The extremist preacher Abdullah al-Muhaysini no longer has to worry about US sanctions. In late August 2026, the US Department of the Treasury removed the former jihadist from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list, or SDN List. It includes individuals and organizations whose assets are frozen in the US and with whom US citizens are generally not allowed to do business.
After Syria’s civil war broke out in 2011, al-Muhaysini recruited fighters and helped establish a governing structure shaped by the Nusra Front, which emerged from al-Qaeda.
His removal from the list is linked to the new US government policy on Syria: Washington also removed the Nusra Front and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) from the SDN List.

25 years after the September 11 attacks, this is a remarkable snapshot. Al-Qaeda — which means “the base” in Arabic — has neither disappeared nor remained the same organization: Its core has weakened, but its regional branches have remained strong across parts of Africa and Asia, observers agree.
Regional offshoots in the Sahel, Yemen and Afghanistan
Only, al-Qaeda itself is operating less and less under its own name.
“This is largely due to the successful counterterrorism efforts following 2001,” Lars Berger, professor of terrorism studies at the German Federal University of Administrative Sciences, told DW.
The military campaign in Afghanistan, along with cooperation between intelligence agencies and police, has significantly weakened the group.
“From this perspective, the September 11 attacks were a major strategic failure for al-Qaeda,” Berger said.

The hoped-for radicalization of the Arab world and the overthrow of its regimes failed to materialize. About ten years after the attacks in New York and Washington, al-Qaeda’s most famous figure, Osama bin Laden, was killed in May 2011.
As a result, al-Qaeda reorganized itself.

“The militia sought out areas where it could establish a permanent foothold, for example in parts of Africa or Yemen,” Berger said, adding that “countries with weak state structures, overwhelmed security forces and unresolved local conflicts are particularly favorable.”
“Today, this is particularly true of Africa,” Rüdiger Lohlker, professor emeritus of Islamic studies at the University of Vienna, notes.

blocks.caption: Fighters of the al-Qaeda offshoot al-Shabab are gaining a foothold in the Sahel regionImage: Badri Media/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the Sahel, Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM, has emerged as a powerful al-Qaeda offshoot, he said.

An analysis by the think tank Critical Threats Project uses Niger as an example to show how JNIM and the Islamic State’s Sahel Province (ISSP) compete for territory, fighters and resources. In June 2026, JNIM claimed responsibility for an attack on the international airport in Niger’s capital, Niamey.

In Somalia, al-Shabab — a group closely linked to al-Qaeda — is strong, and in Yemen, al-Qaeda is present in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP). Afghanistan also remains a safe haven for the terrorist organization.
However, the success of these offshoots cannot be explained solely by jihadist ideology, Lohlker added.
Rather, it often coincides with a kind of “economy of violence,” he said, noting that “violence including kidnappings, smuggling and looting has long been an economic factor for terrorism.”
He also said that there are veritable “markets for violence:” Where money can be made through violence, jihadist organizations can also recruit and retain followers.
“We fundamentally need to move away from a Eurocentric perspective,” Lohlker further points out.
In his view, al-Qaeda and other jihadist groups have always been far more present outside Europe and the US than it has appeared from a Western perspective.
Al-Qaeda’s regional involvement

However, over the years, the offshoots’ strategies have undergone a change. According to Lars Berger, there has been a “strategic shift” away from direct attacks on the “distant enemy” and toward the establishment of local structures.

“We are now seeing an attempt to proceed in an alternative and gradual manner, namely instead of spectacular acts of violence ordered from the highest levels, there are smaller-scale actions that are more grassroots in nature,” he said.
In the Sahel, this entails forming local alliances, gaining influence in communities, and controlling territories. The Critical Threats Project describes this development as “localization.”

Al-Qaeda is thus surviving precisely through this differentiation. JNIM capitalizes on ethnic and social conflicts in the Sahel, while al-Shabaab exploits conflicts within Somali clan structures. The global jihadist goal remains as an ideological framework, but the actual fighting takes place on the ground.

blocks.caption: Ten years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden was killed. Since then, the group has lost visibility but not regional influence through their proxies (file photo from 2001)Image: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Al-Qaeda competes with the “Islamic State”
In the competition for public attention, however, al-Qaeda faces a superior rival: the so-called “Islamic State,” or IS.

“Ultimately, younger jihadists tend to be more drawn to the ‘Islamic State,'” terrorism expert Behnam Heidenreuter-Said, head of the research center for Strategic Police Research at the Hamburg Police Academy, told DW.
IS has carried out “more spectacular” and media-effective terrorist attacks, he said, highlighting that “al-Qaeda has taken a more long-term approach.”
Heidenreuter-Said, who published a comprehensive history of al-Qaeda in 2018, added that “IS wanted to make a splash and demonstrate successes as quickly as possible in order to grow explosively.”
However, IS’s expansion was followed by its collapse, he said. Al-Qaeda, on the other hand, continues to exist, albeit under changed circumstances.
Shortage of al-Qaeda updates

The terrorist group meanwhile faces the question of whether it can replace its aging fighters. Although this is conceivable, al-Qaeda as a brand is visibly fading, Heidenreuter-Said observed. In Europe in particular, militant jihadism has become less attractive. However, jihadist ideas have not disappeared, al-Qaeda has simply lost its former ability to mobilize large numbers of young people, he said.
It is hard to say just how dangerous the organization actually still is, Behnam Heidenreuter-Said points out.
“Everyone agrees that there is currently virtually no information about al-Qaeda and we simply don’t know what it is doing right now,” he said.

Furthermore, since the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, it has been striking how little al-Qaeda has been visible in the major regional conflicts, he said. In his view, Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran have dominated the political and military stage. /dl

articles.title: 'She's back': Fans dance, sing and cry after Céline Dion's comeback concert in Paris
articles.summary: Thousands turned out to witness Céline Dion perform in Paris on Saturday, her first show after a six year illness-induced hiatus.

blocks.text: Céline Dion's first concert in years delighted fans, with the Canadian singer crying as she made an emotional comeback to the stage.
It was Dion's first full concert in six years after she was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome, which forced her to cancel tours.
Joyful fans spilled out of the Paris La Défense Arena on Saturday night singing and dancing to her classic hits, while some were still wiping away tears.
Paris correspondent Hugh Schofield went along and reflects on getting swept up in the Dion dalliance that French fans are calling "the biggest comeback since Charles de Gaulle".

articles.title: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'high-stakes' comeback show in Paris
articles.summary: The iconic Canadian singer kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.

blocks.text: "I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return.
"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said.
"I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.
She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry."
"But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."
They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.
Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year.
The Mirror's Lucy Needham, external noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return".
"Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."

After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".
The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick, external.
She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."

"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."
She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.
"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.

But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."
Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), external, said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.
She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."
Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.
Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London, external writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".
She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.
"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.
The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".

"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.
"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety., external

In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."
The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.
"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine, external in 2024.
"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."
When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.
The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.
Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.
Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.
Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.
Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.

"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.
Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.
And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

articles.title: One dead and more than 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast in rough seas
articles.summary:
Prime minister’s office tells families of those missing ‘the nation stands with you’ as search and rescue efforts continue

One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank…

blocks.text: One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the country’s government says.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail with more than 40 passengers and crew on Friday from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones,” Vanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office said in a statement on Sunday.
“Search and rescue operations are continuing.”
Fifteen of those onboard have been “accounted for alive” and one body has been recovered, the statement said.
“Over 30 people remain missing at sea,” it said.
“To the survivors, we ⁠pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of ​those ​missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands ​with you ‌in this time ​of ​grief.”
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in New Caledonia said it was assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
Matai Seremaiah, the member of parliament for Luganville who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the south-east coast where currents may have carried survivors.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: PH joins India-led coalition to boost disaster-resilient infrastructure
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is turning to an India-led global coalition for technical expertise and possible financing to build infrastructure that can better withstand floods and other…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is turning to an India-led global coalition for technical expertise and possible financing to build infrastructure that can better withstand floods and other disasters, according to Malacañang.
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Saturday met with officials of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in New Delhi as Manila formally joined the group as its 71st member.
Marcos is currently in India to attend the 18th Brics Summit as this year’s chair of the Association of the Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The membership comes as the Marcos administration faces growing pressure to improve the country’s flood-control and other disaster mitigation infrastructure amid increasingly adverse weather events worsened by climate change.

Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Secretary Dave Gomez said the CDRI could help the Philippines learn from other countries how to design and build roads, bridges and ports that can withstand disasters and climate-related risks.
“First and foremost, they will teach us—this is essentially a sharing of experiences among coalition members on how to deal with disasters and how to build disaster resilience,” Gomez said.
The coalition could also help the Philippines access financing for projects meant to make infrastructure more resilient, he added.
According to Gomez, investing in stronger infrastructure before disasters strike would be more beneficial in the long run than spending heavily on reconstruction and recovery after calamities.

The Philippines has been dealing with recurring flooding, particularly in Metro Manila and other urban and low-lying areas, with the government pursuing large-scale flood-control and drainage projects while also reviewing existing infrastructure.

The CDRI membership provides the Philippines an opportunity to tap the experience of other countries in addressing such challenges, particularly in designing infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather and other hazards.
CDRI Director-General Amit Prothi welcomed the Philippines’ membership and said he looks forward to working with Philippine institutions on disaster-resilient infrastructure.
He cited the Philippines’ extensive experience and knowledge in dealing with flooding, earthquakes and volcanic activity.
Knowledge sharing

Prothi said the country’s long-standing efforts to address these challenges could provide valuable lessons for other countries, especially in its experience in disaster risk management, preparedness, response, and resilient recovery.

Launched by the Indian government in 2019, the CDRI is a voluntary and nonbinding global partnership that brings together governments, international organizations, financial institutions, private companies and academic institutions.
It seeks to promote the sharing of expertise and best practices, strengthen technical capabilities and encourage investments in infrastructure that can withstand disasters and climate change.

The coalition also focuses on shaping policies and financing, integrating risk-aware development, scaling up resilience actions, and building stakeholder capacity to protect vulnerable communities and high-risk regions.
$10 trillion global investment

By 2050, CDRI aims to drive $10 trillion in resilient infrastructure investments and services to improve environmental quality, livelihoods and well-being for more than three billion people worldwide.
Overall, the CDRI is composed of 71 members, including 59 countries and 12 partner organizations.
The Philippines is the second Southeast Asian country to join the coalition after Vietnam.
The Department of Public Works and Highways has been designated to represent the Philippines in the CDRI.

The country’s participation in CDRI also forms part of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and aligns with the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028, the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2023-2050, and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (NDRRMP) 2020-2030. /gsg
/gsg

articles.title: Zelensky offers to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders’ summit scheduled for December.…

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders’ summit scheduled for December.
Zelenskyy replied enthusiastically when DW’s correspondent Misha Komadovsky posed the question on Friday.
“Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he said.
Zelenskyy added that what he was going to say to Putin mattered less than results.
“It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. […] Results matter. That’s it.”
Zelenskyy and Putin have not met in person since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbor in February 2022.
The Kremlin has so far declined to say whether Putin would go to Miami for the meeting.
The Russian leader has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019.
Last month, Russia’s Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was however invited by the US to attend a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina in a move that upset European officials.
100-year partnership declaration with Canada
First up, however, Zelenskyy spoke of the deals he signed on Thursday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, including a 100-year partnership declaration.

Zelenskyy underlined the importance of the deal, which he said covered numerous sectors, “from security, financing, energy, very important energy, veteran policy, and culture, and relationships and humanitarian issues.”
“So it’s a global decision, a really historic decision, and I’m happy that we have it,” he said.
Zelenskyy said he had also signed a deal on collaboration on drone production with the Canadian leader involving a number of Ukrainian companies.
Zelenskyy pushes for more Patriot missiles ahead of winter
Zelenskyy’s interview with DW comes as summer is nearly over and Ukraine is gearing up for the cold months of winter.
The Ukrainian president has conceded that his country has been struggling to counter flying jet-propelled drones that Russia has been increasingly deploying.
“They [US] have political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big. So it means that stocks is a variant,” he said.
“Will Americans be ready to give us (Patriots)? I don’t know. We will see.”
Patriot missiles are powerful weapons that are currently the most effective defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
What Zelenskyy needs from US and European allies
“Russia [currently] produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need a 1-to-2 [ratio], 280 missiles,” Zelenskyy told DW.

“You will never have 280 missiles per month, and between us, it’s a huge challenge to have [even] 100 missiles per month. This is what I want. I want to have 100-120 for these difficult months, especially the cold months.”
Germany earlier this week said it was going to send Patriot missiles from its national stock, without specifying how many missiles that would be.
Zelenskyy called on Kyiv’s European allies to provide more support.
“They have to give as much as possible. With all respect to them, they have to give to Ukrainians to save their lives.”
Zelenskyy also spoke of having secured agreements with several European companies to develop a Ukrainian-led anti-missile system called Freya.
He said he was hoping that the first test phase would begin by the end of December, stressing that time was short.
Ukraine in ‘good position for negotiations’
Zelenskyy said that it was a “good signal” that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier this week, and not just Moscow.
He said he had made clear to them that his country was well-placed for negotiations on ending the conflict, with Russia estimated to be losing more than 30,000 soldiers a month.
Zelenskyy said this meant that Moscow was paying a “big price” for small gains on the battlefield.
“So that’s why we think that we have now good position for negotiations,” he said, adding that his country was stronger than last year.

blocks.caption: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in KyivImage: Ukrainian Presidential Press Office/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Grain and energy top priorities
The other concern that has been coming up steadily over this summer is the shipment of grains through the Black Sea, with Moscow and Kyiv currently targeting each other’s ships and hindering exports.
Russia’s de facto blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports in the Odesa region has led to a 76% fall in Ukraine’s grain exports year-on-year so far in August.
Zelenskyy said he had spoken with the two envoys about an energy and grain ceasefire that could provide a starting point for peace.
“What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve,” he said.

Misha Komadovsky US Correspondent Roshni Majumdar Roshni is a global breaking news writer and digital editor for DW, based in Germany. Timothy Jones Writer, translator and editor with DW’s online news team.

articles.title: India’s BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
articles.summary: India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019. The summit comes…

blocks.text: India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi’s year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi’s diplomatic gains.
New Delhi and Beijing locked in ‘armed coexistence’ and competition
Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.
Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India’s engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi’s longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.
“These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers,” Kantha told DW.
However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

blocks.caption: India’s geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powersImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.
The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.
Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

“The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard,” said Kantha.

“It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple ‘elephant and dragon’ story,” he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world’s two most populous nations.
BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow
India’s presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

blocks.caption: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit

blocks.text: With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.
Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair’s statement instead.
With Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

“Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground,” says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.
“BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common,” he added.
Fears of Chinese dominance
The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.
“Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation,” Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking ‘de-dollarization.'”
“Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements.”
India’s ‘America Plus’ strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.
India’s diplomatic course is not a pure “multi-alignment” approach but an “America Plus” strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

“India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons,” said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.
But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.
“A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia’s growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance,” he said.
In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India’s power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform. /dl

articles.title: Trump while in Ireland: Reunification would be ‘fantastic’
articles.summary: DUBLIN — US President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” as he waded into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a…

blocks.text: DUBLIN — US President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” as he waded into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a tournament at his Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the United Kingdom’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told a reporter who sought his opinion on the issue. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” the Republican president said, adding that “the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”
The Irish unity debate is heated
Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether Irish or British — drove decades of violence in the six-county region that has a Protestant majority and has remained part of the U.K.
Previous American presidents, including Democrat Joe Biden, who has strong emotional ties to Ireland, have avoided commenting directly on the subject.

Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbor Britain, became a self-governing Catholic-majority country a century ago. Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists, most of them Catholic, who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.

A 1998 peace accord that the United States was instrumental in negotiating largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved. That agreement allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the U.K. would only consider allowing a referendum “when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered.” Burnham’s office referred back to that comment when asked about Trump’s statement.

Trump’s comments Saturday, along with recent statements about the Falkland Islands, a small British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean that Argentina calls Las Malvinas, could also be viewed as a dig at Britain, given his anger over London’s refusal to be drawn into the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Trump also talked about the Falkland Islands

Trump once more raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falklands. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has recently restated his country’s claim to the territory of about 3,500 people, which is about 300 miles (480 kilometers) east of the southeast coast of Argentina.

Trump has previously said Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. On Saturday, he expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the Falklands as it did after Argentina invaded in 1982.
“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out,” he said.
A meeting with the Irish president who criticized Trump

Trump also held talks in Dublin with Irish President Catherine Connolly, a left-wing politician who joined protesters when Trump visited Ireland in 2019 during his first term in office. She is now Ireland’s elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, Connolly has in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a “bully.”

blocks.caption: Protesters show placards during a demonstration against the visit of U.S. President Donald Trump in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. Associated Press

blocks.text: Connolly said in a statement after the meeting that she conveyed to Trump “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalization of war and genocide can never be accepted.” She gave Trump several gifts, among them a collection by the late Irish poet Michael Longley that includes the sonnet “Ceasefire.”
Asked about the meeting, Trump first had his protocol chief, Monica Crowley, answer before he was pressed and said it was “very nice.” “We discussed a lot of things, quickly,” Trump said.
Trump’s presence irks some Dubliners
Police put up a cordon around Dublin’s 1,750-acre (700-hectare) Phoenix Park, where Connolly, Martin and U.S. Ambassador Edward Walsh have residences and welcomed Trump.
A protest march drew thousands to central Dublin. He had left the city and was on the way to his Doonbeg golf course on the country’s Atlantic coast by the time the demonstration began.
Many in the crowd waved Irish or Palestinian flags and chanted “Donald Trump not welcome here” and “Irish government, shame on you!”
Paula Butler said she came with a contingent from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre to oppose the American president’s “attitude to women, to refugees, to migrants.”
She was unimpressed by Trump’s support for Irish unity, a popular cause in Ireland.
“What he knows about Irish unity, I’d say I know more on my little finger,” Butler said.
Kim Mathis, who moved from Florida to Dublin last year with her partner, said “part of the reason we moved to Ireland was to get away from Trump and all of his horrific policies.”
She said dealing with Trump is “a global conundrum” for governments. “It would be really nice if politicians would just say, ‘Stay home.'”
Eric Trump defends family’s presence in Ireland
Speaking to Irish national broadcaster RTE on Friday in Doonbeg, Trump’s son Eric said the course is the largest employer in the area.

“Go down to Morrissey’s tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family, go have them attest to what we’ve done for the country and what we’ve invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them,” he said.
Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.

He spends most weekends playing golf at his clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. During that visit, he held talks with the British prime minister and the president of the European Commission.
Asked if he would return to Ireland next year for the Ryder Cup, Trump said, “I will. Absolutely.” /dl

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces
articles.summary:
Iran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi Arabia

Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used…

blocks.text: Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces led growing numbers of civilians to flee.

The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X.
The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh.
On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the south-western part of the country.
“Air Force of the Armed Forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said Sunday in a post on X.
