articles.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
articles.summary: The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fears about the reliability of the US, but equally important is the need to keep gold closer to home in the…

image.caption: In an age of geopolitical unrest, more and more countries want to have easy access to their gold reservesImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where about half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security.
To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the United States as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane.

The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move about 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis.
The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness."

France also removed its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that it was not politically motivated.

blocks.caption: The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of EnglandImage: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS

blocks.text: Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves, respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns about the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy toward the European Union, including threats to annex part of Greenland.
The gold rush

Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, told DW the outright seizure of assets is an "extremely remote risk" for European central banks. However, he said, there are growing concerns about ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty.
"The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he said.

In general, said Krishnan Gopaul, of the World Gold Council, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs.

A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-tonne average over the preceding decade.

Because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign-debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset, Gopaul said.
"As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he said.

The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the United States and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis.

Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location.
"Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximize resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," Tillett said.

Gopaul said reserve management had become "incredibly important" and that, while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure that the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub that moves fast.
He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the United Kingdom is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market."

"The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he said. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold."
The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion).
The US question

While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making.
Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries.
That decision seems to be driven by concern about US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors.
Tillett said gold remained sensitive to decisions by the US Federal Reserve and general concern about US financial markets meant that gold holders are looking to move their assets.

As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric about Greenland and continued veiled threats toward the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around.

blocks.caption: US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leadersImage: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Yet the United States, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan, in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved about 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the United States.
Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves."

articles.title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide
articles.summary:
Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more…

blocks.text: Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.

Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.
The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.

Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”

UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.

Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.
“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.

Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.

The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.

Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.

“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”
after newsletter promotion

She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”
Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.

“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.
“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”

FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.
A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

articles.title: 'It was heartbreaking'- Americans remember what they were doing on 9/11
articles.summary: The BBC asks people in Washington what they were doing on that day and how 11 September 2001 changed the country.

blocks.text: On Tuesday 11 September 2001, hijackers seized US passenger jets and crashed them into two New York skyscrapers, killing thousands of people.
A third plane destroyed the western face of the Pentagon - the giant headquarters of the US military just outside the nation's capital, Washington DC.
The fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. It is thought the hijackers had meant to attack Washington's Capitol Building.
The BBC spoke to Americans in Washington about what they were doing on that day and how 9/11 has changed the country.

articles.summary:
Canadian PM Mark Carney hosts president in Calgary, where he grew up alongside large Ukrainian community

Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish…

blocks.text: Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.
“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.
The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.
That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.
“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.
In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.
“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.

The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.
Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.
Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.
The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.
Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.
Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”
Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.

But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.
“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.
“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”
After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.
He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.

articles.title: TV presenter v secret son: the succession dispute engulfing a Ugandan kingdom
articles.summary:
Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reveal son’s existence as they reject committee’s choice of cousin as new monarch

A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.

blocks.caption: King Oyo Nyimba, aged 13, sits between his mother Best Kemigisha and an unidentified adviser during celebrations marking his first decade in power in Fort Portal, Uganda. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.

However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.

blocks.caption: Princess Ruth Komuntale waiting to receive the body of her brother, the late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at Entebbe International airport last week. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”

In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.

blocks.caption: A portrait of the late king on the red carpet at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.
“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.

The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.

blocks.caption: Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki waiting to receive the body of her son at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.

The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.
“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”

blocks.caption: Uganda’s president, Yoweri Museveni, lays a wreath on the casket of the king at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.
Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.

Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.
In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.

blocks.caption: The casket of the late king arrives at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: ‘Our forefathers are coming back’: Naga people celebrate after Oxford museum agrees to return remains
articles.summary:
Following six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east India

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland,…

blocks.text: Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.

On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”

Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.

The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.

blocks.caption: Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist (kneeling, centre, in a red scarf) with other Naga delegates and museum staff.  Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”

In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.

“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”

The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.

blocks.caption: Members of the Naga delegation view the relics on display at the Pitt Rivers Museum. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: “They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”

Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

articles.title: Rubio says US will work with allies to stop drug-trafficking as three killed in latest boat strike
articles.summary:
Rubio visits Ecuador and welcomes cooperation after campaign of unilateral strikes on alleged ‘narco-terrorists’

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward…

blocks.text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”

The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.

Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.

Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.

“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.
He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.

Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then the US military blows up the vessels.
The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

articles.title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
articles.summary:
Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking

The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which

blocks.text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.
Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.

“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.

The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.

Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.

In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.
During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.

On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.

Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel Noboa  Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.

During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government.
During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.

Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

articles.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
articles.summary:
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’

Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the…

blocks.text: Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.

Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.

When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”

The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.

Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”

The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.

The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.

Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.
The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators
articles.summary:
Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January

The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in…

blocks.text: The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.

Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.

In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.
The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.
At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.

The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.
In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.

“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.

It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.

“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”

Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.

“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.

It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.

“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”
In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.
A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.
“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.
“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”
Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.
Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

articles.title: 3 suspects in Degamo slay found guilty of illegal possession of gun, bombs
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—A Manila court has found three former Army soldiers, who were earlier linked to the killing of former Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo, guilty of illegal possession of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—A Manila court has found three former Army soldiers, who were earlier linked to the killing of former Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo, guilty of illegal possession of firearms and explosives.
Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 40, in an Aug. 18 decision, convicted Joric Labrador of unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition.
It also found Joven Javier and Benjie Rodriguez guilty of one count each of unlawful possession of explosives in connection with the assassination of Degamo in March 2023.
Labrador was sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, while Javier and Rodriguez were meted a prison term of reclusion perpetua or 20 years.

The court also directed that the firearm and explosives seized from the three accused be handed over to the Philippine National Police.These items include a .45 caliber pistol, two magazines, 14 rounds of live ammunition, and two hand grenades,
The three respondents are also facing multiple murder and frustrated murder and attempted murder charges before the Manila RTC for the killing of Degamo.
The 56-year-old governor was shot down inside his home in Pamploma town, Negros Oriental.
According to the Department of Justice, which brought the charges to the Manila RTC, the validity of warrantless arrests was upheld in these cases.
This is because the confiscated items were properly identified and handled, based on testimonies by the police and other witnesses. /apl

articles.title: DPWH chief Dizon to testify in graft trial of Zaldy Co, others
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon will testify in the trial of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and his co-accused on graft charges in connection with alleged anomalous…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon will testify in the trial of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and his co-accused on graft charges in connection with alleged anomalous flood control project in Mindoro, the Sandiganbayan said on Wednesday.

Associate Justice Maryann Corpuz-Mañalac made this announcement as the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division heard testimonies from two cashier officers of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Mimaropa (Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan).
“As agreed upon, let the presentation of the next witness in the person of Secretary Vince Dizon proceed on September 23, at 8:30 in the morning,” Corpuz-Mañalac.
Corpuz-Mañalac also said the next witness’ judicial affidavit has been submitted online to the court.

In November 2025, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division issued arrest warrants against Co and his co-accused from the DPWH and Sunwest Corporation in connection with a P289.9 million road dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, which was flagged as substandard and found to have structural deficiencies.
Co was linked to Sunwest Corporation, which was among the top 15 contractors awarded with the most flood control projects worth P100 billion from July 2022 to May 2025. /gsg

articles.title: NPA leader killed in clash with Army troops in Leyte
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY- A ranking New People’s Army (NPA) leader was killed in a brief clash with government troops on Tuesday afternoon in the hinterlands of Barangay Caridad, Baybay City, Leyte, the…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY- A ranking New People’s Army (NPA) leader was killed in a brief clash with government troops on Tuesday afternoon in the hinterlands of Barangay Caridad, Baybay City, Leyte, the military reported.

The Army’s 8th Infantry Division(ID), which is based in Catbalogan City, Samar, said the encounter occurred on Sept. 8 after soldiers received information from a resident about the presence of armed men allegedly collecting money and food from communities in the area.
Troops from the 802nd Infantry Brigade(IB) proceeded to the area to verify the report, resulting in a firefight that lasted about five minutes, according to the military.
Killed was Erwin Murillo Maceda, alias “Romnick,” who was identified by the Army as the vice team leader of the NPA’s Island Committee Levox under the Eastern Visayas Regional Party Committee.
An M16 rifle was also recovered from the encounter site, the 8th ID said.

Brig. Gen. Pompeyo Jason Almagro, commander of the 802nd IB, said Maceda and his group had allegedly been involved in extortion, threats against residents and business owners, and attacks on government security installations in Leyte.

“The people of Leyte have endured years of fear, intimidation, and disruption caused by armed groups. We will not allow these conditions to return to communities that have worked hard to achieve peace,” Almagro said in a statement released on Wednesday.

The military said the encounter followed reports of armed NPA members attempting to regain their presence in communities where government authorities have declared stable peace and security conditions.
The Army also credited residents’ cooperation and timely reporting for enabling government forces to respond to the reported presence of armed men.
“The cooperation of our communities is critical. Their timely reporting allows government forces to respond before threats can escalate,” Almagro said.
The 8th ID renewed its call for remaining NPA members to abandon armed struggle and surrender, saying government programs are available to assist former rebels who return to civilian life.
The military said it would continue operations in areas where armed groups are reported to be operating while encouraging NPA members to return peacefully to their families and communities./coa
